Stage 3 — introduce a throwing effect, with no protection. This is what every Vue 3.6 pre-release actually shipped, from 3.6.0-alpha.1 through 3.6.0-rc.9:

const good1 = makeEffect(() => console.log('good watcher A ran'))
const bad = makeEffect(() => { throw new Error('getter blew up') })
const good2 = makeEffect(() => console.log('good watcher B ran'))

queue(good1)
queue(bad)
queue(good2)

flush()
// good watcher A ran
// Uncaught Error: getter blew up
// (good watcher B never ran — and notifyIndex/notifyBufferLength
//  were left pointing mid-buffer, non-zero)

Walk through exactly what happened: good1.notify() runs and returns normally, notifyIndex advances to 1. bad.notify() throws. Because there's no try/catch around the call, the exception propagates straight out of the while loop — skipping the two lines that reset notifyIndex and notifyBufferLength to 0. good2 was already sitting in the buffer, but the loop never reaches it. The buffer isn't empty and the index isn't reset — it's just abandoned, mid-walk, with good2 still inside it.

The next time any write anywhere calls flush() again, the while (notifyIndex < notifyBufferLength) check is still true from the leftover state, so the loop picks up right where it left off and finally calls good2.notify() — attached to whatever unrelated write happened to trigger that next flush. That's the exact bug from the opening example.

Stage 4 — the fix, isolating each notify call. This is what shipped in 3.6.0-rc.10, restoring 3.5's behavior:

function flush() {
  let hasError = false
  let error
  while (notifyIndex < notifyBufferLength) {
    const effect = notifyBuffer[notifyIndex]
    notifyBuffer[notifyIndex++] = undefined
    try {
      effect.notify()
    } catch (e) {
      if (!hasError) {
        hasError = true
        error = e
      }
    }
  }
  notifyIndex = 0
  notifyBufferLength = 0
  if (hasError) throw error
}

Key concept: a single try/catch wraps each individual effect.notify() call, so a throw from one effect can't stop the loop from reaching the next one — the loop itself can no longer throw at all. That's what makes the reset lines right after the loop unconditional: there's no uncaught exception left to jump past them, so notifyIndex and notifyBufferLength always get reset to zero before the next write's flush. Only the first error that occurred is remembered, in hasError/error, and rethrown once every queued effect has had its turn.

Run the stage-3 example through this version and good2 ran prints immediately, in the same flush as the throw — and the error still surfaces to whoever triggered the write, just after everyone's had their notify.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Two throwing effects in the same batch. Only the first error is captured and rethrown; the second (and any later) thrower still gets its notify() call — so its side effects before the throw statement still happen — but its exception is silently discarded. If you need to know about every failure in a batch, don't rely on the single rethrown error; catch inside each effect instead (see Best Practices).
  • flush: 'sync' isn't required for this to matter. The examples use it to make ordering legible on paper, but default ('pre') and 'post' watchers are notified through this exact same buffer and loop — they're just queued by a component-level scheduler job that itself sits in the buffer, rather than running immediately. A throw anywhere in that chain goes through the same per-effect try/catch logic described above.
  • This was never a stable-release bug, but it was a long-lived pre-release one. It's worth repeating because version confusion is exactly how stale advice spreads in a framework ecosystem: 3.5.x never had it — it predates the alien-signals rewrite entirely — and it never reached a non-RC 3.6.0 release. But it wasn't confined to rc.9 either: the unprotected flush() shipped unchanged from 3.6.0-alpha.1 all the way through 3.6.0-rc.9, and was only fixed in rc.10. If you're pinned to an exact 3.6 pre-release for testing, pin to rc.10 or later.
  • app.config.errorHandler still fires for the thrown error either way — this bug was never about error reporting going missing, only about a sibling effect's execution being delayed. Don't confuse "I got an error callback" with "every watcher that should have run, ran."
  • A computed's own dirty flag isn't affected by this. The computed in the opening example (label) correctly stays dirty and will recompute (and rethrow) on its next read regardless of this bug; what the bug delayed was the other watcher, not the throwing one.

Best Practices

  • Don't let a risky computed or watcher getter run unguarded if a sibling's correctness depends on timing. Wrap the risky part in its own try/catch and fall back to a safe value, rather than letting the exception travel up into Vue's flush loop at all: 
  const label = computed(() => {
    try {
      return user.value.name.toUpperCase()
    } catch {
      return '—'
    }
  })
  • Treat watchers on the same source as independent, not ordered. Even with the fix, only the first error in a batch is rethrown — you cannot depend on "if watcher A didn't throw, I'll find out about watcher B's error the same way." Each effect's failure handling is its own responsibility.
  • Use app.config.errorHandler for centralized reporting, not as a substitute for per-watcher guards — it tells you that something threw, not which of several effects in the same batch also ran cleanly.
  • If you're testing against a 3.6 release candidate today, pin to rc.10 or newer. npm view vue dist-tags tells you the current rc tag; don't trust a cached node_modules from a few weeks ago to reflect it.

FAQ

Does this bug affect Vue 3.5?

No. It came in with the alien-signals-based reactivity rewrite that's exclusive to the 3.6 line — 3.5.x doesn't run this code at all, and every 3.5.x release behaves like the fixed version described in Stage 4. Within 3.6, the bug wasn't limited to rc.9 either: the unprotected flush() shipped unchanged from 3.6.0-alpha.1 through 3.6.0-rc.9, and was fixed in 3.6.0-rc.10.

Is the batch described here the same as the nextTick queue?

No — they're adjacent, not the same thing. nextTick schedules component re-renders on a microtask so the DOM updates once per tick. The notify buffer in this article is the layer underneath: a component's render job is itself one effect queued into this buffer, alongside your watch and computed effects. flush: 'sync' watchers skip the nextTick scheduling and run directly out of this loop.

Will my component fail to re-render if a sibling watcher throws?

With the fix (3.6.0-rc.10 and later, and all of 3.5), no — your render job still gets its notify() call in the same flush, exactly like good2 in Stage 4. On any unpatched pre-release (3.6.0-alpha.1 through rc.9), it theoretically could, for the same reason any other queued effect could: a throw earlier in the buffer would abandon the loop before reaching it.

Should I stop using watch() and handle everything with try/catch instead?

No — watch() and computed() are still the right tool. The takeaway isn't "avoid the reactivity system," it's "don't assume Vue isolates failures between independent effects for you." Guard the specific logic that can realistically throw, inside the watcher or computed itself.

Where can I read the actual fix?

vuejs/core#15674 has the original repro and root-cause analysis; PR #15676 has the diff that shipped in 3.6.0-rc.10.

Cheat Sheet

What How it behaves
A ref write Marks dependent effects dirty, queues them into a shared notify buffer — does not call them directly
flush() Walks the notify buffer in a loop, calling effect.notify() on each queued effect in order
flush: 'sync' watcher Runs straight out of this loop, with no nextTick scheduling in between
Default ('pre'/'post') watcher Queued through a component-level scheduler job, which is itself just one more effect in the same buffer
One effect throws (3.5, and 3.6 ≥ rc.10) Every other queued effect still runs; the first error is rethrown once the whole batch is drained
One effect throws (any 3.6.0-alpha.1 – rc.9 pre-release) The loop abandons mid-buffer; remaining effects are delivered later, attached to the next unrelated write
Two effects throw in one batch Both still run; only the first effect's error is rethrown, the second's is discarded
app.config.errorHandler Still fires for the thrown error in every version — this was never a reporting bug 
// Defensive pattern: don't depend on Vue isolating failures between effects
const safeValue = computed(() => {
  try {
    return riskyDerivation(source.value)
  } catch (err) {
    app.config.errorHandler?.(err, null, 'computed getter')
    return fallbackValue
  }
})

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Key Takeaways

  • A ref write doesn't call its watchers directly — it queues them into a shared notify buffer, and a single flush() loop walks that buffer afterward.
  • For the entire 3.6 pre-release line, from 3.6.0-alpha.1 through 3.6.0-rc.9, a throw in one effect could abandon that loop mid-walk, silently delaying unrelated effects until the next write. Fixed in 3.6.0-rc.10 (#15674, #15676), matching how 3.5.x always behaved.
  • Even fixed, only the first error in a batch is rethrown to your code — later throwers still execute but their errors are swallowed.
  • Don't rely on Vue to isolate failures between independent watchers or computeds; guard the specific logic that can throw, inside the effect itself.
  • The nextTick DOM queue and this reactivity-level notify buffer are two different layers — your component's render job is just one more effect sitting in the same buffer as your watchers.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

A watcher that "randomly" stops firing isn't random — it's either your own logic or, if you were on a 3.6 pre-release before rc.10, a scheduling gap that's now closed. Either way, the fix is the same: stop assuming Vue hands you isolation you never asked for, and guard the part that can actually throw.

Have you hit a watcher that seemed to miss an update for no reason? Drop what you found in the comments — framework-internals bugs like this one are exactly the kind of thing worth comparing notes on.

That was the day when it was at 0, and now, after 1 month and 10 days, it has lots of features and 11 users!!

But I noticed that users are there, but they barely come back.

So I decided to focus on getting users now.

so what new did i change to achieve this in crowdwide?

there was no common social media feature left to implement at this point!!

so now i just thought that i should call the users back by notifications.

i implemented these:

After 24 hours away: a community question they can answer. It picks an open question that matches their interests and has few replies. If none exists, it sends Today's Question.

After 3 days: the most active discussion matching their interests, plus a line on what's new this week (new posts, members, communities).

After 7 days: a last "what you missed" note with replies, likes, and new followers on their posts, plus top posts. It says it's the last reminder.

Channels: each goes by email, by push if they have push notifications turned on, and as a notification waiting in the app. If there's nothing worth saying, nothing is sent.

and these were for when the user isn't coming back, but if the user comes back, what will he do??

like no task??

so i came up with that... that i should give him some task, like answering any question. not a maths or physics question lol.

i mean a funny, short, concise question.

and u will be able to answer other people's questions too!!

also, the Privacy page now mentions the reminders.

thinking of adding more things now... maybe today you'll see something like streaks and badges... that's under development right now!!

reddit...

also, to get ideas for getting more users, i was checking out other similar platforms that match Crowdwide's category.

like reddit!!

and idk why this happens only to me.

i was on reddit, opened a page on r/startupideaindia, and saw a post from a user saying that he was a tea seller who wanted to get more buyers but wasn't very professional.

he wanted a B2B setup, but he didn't have enough funding and was self-funded, so he was asking for advice and tips.

i commented below with something like:

create hype or try something unique.

like, with tea, provide unique-looking cups or teabags that look normal but show a beautiful picture when dipped in tea.

also, if you're targeting indian people, give them something special on festivals.

like diwali special cups.

india is a price-sensitive market. make them feel like they paid less and got more!!

and they just removed my content, ngl. it was written by me 1000%.

WHYYYY???

so i decided to never implement any useless algorithm on Crowdwide like reddit, which does this.

and while posting the comment, they said i had to wait 3 minutes. i waited 3 mins, then posted it and...

they just removed it for no reason!!

but i also wanted to know how these bots work.

should i implement something like this on Crowdwide??

but fine!!

i don't need bots on Crowdwide.

less users but real users!!

articles.title: Coding Is Easy in 2026. Getting Paid Isn’t. Here’s How to Start.
articles.description: You can build an app.  You can connect a database, add authentication, integrate payments, and put it...
articles.body_html:
You can build an app.

You can connect a database, add authentication, integrate payments, and put it online.

Then you launch.

A few people visit. Someone says, “Looks cool.”

Nobody pays.

What comes between working code and actual income?

A customer with a problem, a useful solution, and a reason to buy.

If you can build software but haven’t earned from it yet, here’s a practical path to your first paying customer.

Step 1: Choose how you want to earn

Start by choosing one route:

Route What you sell Example
Freelancing A finished project Build a booking website
A fixed service The same defined solution to different customers Set up appointment reminders for salons
A software product Access to a tool A monthly repair shop management app

If you need income soon, start by looking for a small paid project. You can sell a clear result to one customer without first building a product for hundreds of people.

If you want a software business, start with one customer anyway. Their workflow will teach you what to build.

Choose one route for now. You can expand later.

Step 2: Pick a customer you can actually reach

“Small businesses” is too broad.

Choose a specific group:

  • Independent repair shop owners.
  • Private tutors.
  • Local cleaning companies.
  • Freelance photographers.
  • Small property owners.

Then ask:

Can I have a conversation with five people in this group?

You might find them through your existing contacts, local businesses, professional communities, or relevant online groups.

Access matters. An audience you can talk to is a useful starting point.

For this guide, let’s use independent repair shops.

Step 3: Find an expensive or frustrating task

Don’t start with:

“Would you use an app I’m building?”

Start with their current work:

  • What do you repeatedly do by hand?
  • What gets forgotten?
  • Where do mistakes cost money?
  • What software do you already pay for?
  • Can you show me how you handled this last time?

Imagine a shop owner tells you:

“We write repair details on paper. Sometimes we forget to follow up with customers who haven’t collected their devices.”

Now you have something specific to investigate.

How often does it happen? How do they handle it today? Is it serious enough to change their process?

Listen for real examples, not polite enthusiasm.

Step 4: Turn the problem into a small offer

“An all-in-one business platform” is difficult to explain and expensive to build.

A smaller offer is easier to understand:

“I’ll set up a repair tracker so you can see open jobs, unpaid balances, and devices waiting for collection.”

Your offer should explain:

  1. Who it helps.
  2. What problem it solves.
  3. What you will deliver.
  4. What it costs.
  5. When it will be ready.

For example:

“I’ll build a repair tracker for your shop with ticket creation, job status, and unpaid balances. The pilot costs $150 and includes setup plus two weeks of support.”

That price is an illustration, not a universal recommendation. Your price needs to reflect the work, customer value, and support involved.

Step 5: Ask for a paid pilot

A compliment tells you someone likes the idea.

A paid agreement gives you stronger evidence that the problem matters.

Ask:

“Would you like to try a paid pilot with those three features?”

Before taking payment, agree in writing on:

  • What is included.
  • The delivery date.
  • The price and payment schedule.
  • How changes will be handled.
  • Support and cancellation terms.

Be clear if the software hasn’t been built yet.

If they decline, ask what is stopping them. It could be the price, timing, trust, or the problem itself.

Use the answer to improve the offer before writing more code.

Step 6: Build one complete workflow

For the repair tracker, your first version might support:

Create ticket → update repair status → record payment → close ticket.

That workflow should work from beginning to end.

You probably don’t need inventory forecasting, staff rankings, ten integrations, and a custom dashboard builder to deliver the agreed pilot.

You do need the basics that make the tool dependable: correct calculations, appropriate access controls, safe handling of customer data, and a way to recover from mistakes.

Keep the feature list small. Make the promised workflow reliable.

Step 7: Help the first customer use it

Sending a login link doesn’t mean the job is finished.

Walk through a real task together.

Watch where the customer pauses:

  • Is a field confusing?
  • Does entering a ticket take too long?
  • Is an important detail missing?
  • Can they find yesterday’s jobs?

Fix the problems that prevent them from getting value.

For a small business tool, setup and support are part of what the customer is buying.

Step 8: Check whether it actually helps

After they’ve used it, ask:

  • Are you still using it?
  • What task became easier?
  • What do you still handle outside the tool?
  • Would you pay to keep using it?
  • Why—or why not?

With their permission, compare the result with how they worked before.

Perhaps they can now find unpaid repairs without checking a stack of paper tickets. That is a concrete benefit you can explain to another shop.

Avoid inventing savings or claiming results you haven’t measured.

A useful customer story is more convincing than a long feature list.

Step 9: Find the next four customers

Use what you learned to approach similar businesses.

Your message can be simple:

“I built a repair tracker that shows open jobs and unpaid balances in one place. How does your shop currently manage those?”

Keep the conversation relevant and personal. Follow community rules and respect people who aren’t interested.

When someone wants a demo, show their main task first. Let them see how the tool would fit their day.

Track a few numbers:

  • People you contacted.
  • Conversations you had.
  • Demos you gave.
  • Customers who paid.
  • Customers who kept using it.

These numbers help you find the problem. Few replies may mean your audience or message needs work. Plenty of demos with no sales may mean the offer needs work.

Step 10: Make sure the money makes sense

Suppose five customers pay $20 per month.

That is $100 in monthly revenue.

Then subtract hosting, payment fees, any paid services, and the time you spend supporting them.

Ask:

“Can I serve more customers at this price without creating an unmanageable job for myself?”

You may need a setup fee, a higher price, a simpler product, or a more limited support offer.

Use recurring pricing when you provide ongoing value. A one-time project may fit a one-time payment better.

Getting paid is the first milestone. Earning sustainably is the next.

A simple plan for your first week

You don’t need to finish a business in seven days. Use the week to replace guesses with evidence.

Day Action
1 Choose one customer group you can reach
2–3 Have five conversations about their current work
4 Pick one repeated problem
5 Write a small offer with a price and clear scope
6 Show a sketch or demo to interested people
7 Ask for a paid pilot and learn from the response

If nobody wants the pilot, investigate before building. Change the problem, customer, or offer based on what you heard.

Before you start your next app

Write down the answers to these questions:

Who will buy it?

What problem will they pay to solve?

How will I reach them?

What is the smallest result I can deliver well?

You don’t need perfect answers. You need answers specific enough to test.

Your first payment might come from a small tool for one local business. Deliver it well, understand why they bought it, and use that knowledge to find the next customer.

What’s harder for you right now: finding a problem, finding customers, or asking them to pay?

articles.title: 226 Scenarios, 43 Detectors, 1 Clean Run: Building a Test Harness That Can't Lie
articles.description: The detectors I didn't trust were the ones that stayed quiet. A rule that fires is easy to...
articles.body_html:
The detectors I didn't trust were the ones that stayed quiet. A rule that fires is easy to sanity-check. A rule that does nothing could mean "checked, found nothing," or "crashed before it checked," and from the outside those look the same.

I ended up with 43 detectors in agentwatch, part of the agentic-suite suite, and this is the harness I built to stop confusing the two. It runs 226 scenarios in about twelve seconds.

The shape of a scenario

Every case is a small dataclass that knows how to build a trace and what should happen to it:

@dataclass
class Scenario:
    id: str
    detector: type
    expect_fire: bool
    build: Callable                     # -> (RunSummary, list[SpanNode])
    severity: str | None = None
    pool: dict[str, Any] | None = None  # scripted DB values
    phase: str = "matrix"               # matrix | precision | llm | clean

The traces are built by hand, not sampled from a corpus, so there's exactly one thing being tested at a time:

add("L1", LoopDetector, True,
    lambda: (summ(total_tool_calls=6), [tool("search_kb") for _ in range(6)]),
    severity="warning")

Six identical calls, threshold of five, should fire a warning. No ambiguity to argue about later.

The traces are hand-built for a reason. A corpus tells you whether the detector fires on real data, but it can't tell you whether it fires for the right reason — corpus traces don't have ground-truth labels. A hand-built trace has exactly one property being tested, and the expected outcome is known before the detector runs. That's the only layer that can compute true TPR and FPR.

Faking the database

Six detectors query Postgres for baselines. Rather than spin up Postgres for the tests, they query a dict:

class ScriptedPool:
    def __init__(self, values=None):
        self.conn = _Conn(values or {})
    def acquire(self):
        return _Acq(self.conn)

The trick is in how the detectors decide whether they have a real pool. _has_valid_pool() checks for an acquire method and not a Mock's return_value — a heuristic that distinguishes a real asyncpg pool from a unittest.mock.Mock. ScriptedPool has acquire but no return_value, so it passes for the real thing and the detectors run their async queries against a dictionary. No Docker, no Postgres, no asyncpg — and about a thousand times faster than spinning up a database container.

The detectors check for an acquire method and not a Mock's return_value, so a ScriptedPool passes for the real thing and runs its async queries against a dictionary.

add("CV1", CostVsBaselineDetector, True,
    lambda: (summ(agent_version="v1", estimated_cost=6.0), []),
    severity="warning", pool={"avg_cost": 2.5})   # baseline $2.50, run $6.00

No Docker, no Postgres, and about a thousand times faster.

Real calls, not mocks

The twelve LLM scenarios hit a real model. This matters, because a mock always returns something valid and can never show you an endpoint that's down — which is exactly the bug that had been hiding in my suite for weeks. So each scenario snapshots the client's counters before and after:

stats_before = dict(client._stats)
anomaly = await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None)
stats_after = dict(client._stats)

llm_calls = stats_after["chat_calls"] - stats_before["chat_calls"]
embed_calls = stats_after["embed_calls"] - stats_before["embed_calls"]

That delta is what lets the harness ask the question that matters.

Six checks, not one

Most detector suites check one thing. This one checks six: did it fire, was the severity right, was it the right detector, was there an explanation, was there an evidence dict, and — the one I care about most — was the model actually called.

tip: A negative case where the model was never called is not a pass. It's a skip wearing a pass. Assert that the dependency ran, not just that the output looked right.

There's a seventh for LLM cases too: parse the model's JSON and confirm its verdict matches what was expected, so a detector can't fire for the wrong reason. For a positive case, the model should say {"hallucination": true}. For a negative, {"hallucination": false}. If the detector fires but the model's verdict disagrees, the detector has a logic bug — it fired for the wrong reason. Verdict matching catches that.

The phase design

The 226 scenarios split into four phases, each catching a different class of bug:

Phase Cases What it catches
matrix 166 (154 ported + 12 hook patterns) Per-detector fire/no-fire and severity
precision 48 (n−1 vs n for 24 thresholds) Off-by-one and floating-point at boundaries
llm 12 (6 LLM detectors, real calls) Silent skips, verdict mismatches
clean 1 (43 detectors, 1 normal trace) False positives on clean input

The matrix phase is the ported predecessor suite — 154 scenarios from the original 35-detector field-test plan, plus 12 new Claude Code hook-pattern detectors. These are the "does it fire when it should" cases, and they're the layer most suites stop at.

The precision phase exists because numeric thresholds live at the boundary. Testing only at n+5 misses off-by-one errors; testing only at n hits floating-point. Two cases per threshold — one below, one at the line — catch both. Forty-eight cases across twenty-four thresholds, and that's the layer that caught the 6/9 ÷ 3/9 = 1.9999... floating-point bug.

The LLM phase is the one that needs real calls, and the one the llm_called_ok check lives in. Mocks would make this phase pass vacuously — a mock always returns a valid response, so a detector that silently fails looks like it works.

The clean phase is one case — all 43 detectors against a single known-normal trace, expecting zero fires. It's the cheapest test in the harness and the most valuable, and it gets its own article in this series.

Boundary cases

For every numeric threshold, two cases — one just below and one at the line:

prec("P-loop-4", LoopDetector, False, _tools(["search_kb"] * 4))              # under
prec("P-loop-5", LoopDetector, True,  _tools(["search_kb"] * 5), "warning")   # at
prec("P-cost-500", CostSpikeDetector, False, lambda: (summ(estimated_cost=5.0), []))
prec("P-cost-501", CostSpikeDetector, True,  lambda: (summ(estimated_cost=5.01), []))

The CostSpikeDetector uses a strict > comparison, so 5.0 doesn't fire (not > 5.0) and 5.01 does. Testing at exactly 5.0 confirms the strictness; testing at 5.01 confirms the threshold. Without both, a >= that should be > slips through.

tip: Test at n−1 and at n for every numeric threshold. The exact boundary is where off-by-one and floating-point bugs live. A test at n+5 proves the detector can fire; it says nothing about where the threshold actually is.

The clean-run check

All 43 detectors against a single known-normal trace, expecting zero fires. The clean trace has three different tools, one-second gaps, a success status, twelve cents of cost, and a 200-character output — every value far from every threshold. If anything fires, it's a false positive, full stop.

async def run_clean():
    summary, spans = _clean_trace()
    fired = [det.anomaly_type
             for det in create_all_detectors()
             if await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None) is not None]
    return {"detectors": 43, "fired": fired, "ok": not fired}

It comes back empty. The full story of why this check matters — and the predecessor data that made it non-negotiable — is in the next piece in this series.

Why it holds up

The rule-based cases run in about four milliseconds. The twelve model calls take a second each and dominate the total, which is still fine for CI. The whole thing ends at 226 of 226, with a hundred percent true-positive rate and zero false positives on the clean trace.

The severity distribution across the matrix cases: 47 warning, 26 critical, 4 info, 77 silent (no anomaly). Every severity matched. The LLM telemetry across the 12 real-call scenarios: 12 chat calls, 100% JSON parse success, latency p50 ≈ 606 ms, p99 ≈ 1427 ms. All LLM request/response I/O is captured in llm-scenario-io.jsonl — 13 records with prompts, system messages, raw responses, model names, and timing. That's the audit trail: the exact thing the model said for each scenario, preserved.

The design choices that did the work were unglamorous: hand-built traces instead of a corpus, a fake database instead of a real one, real model calls instead of mocks, two cases per threshold, and the boring clean trace almost nobody writes.

The harness is checked in at scenario_validation.py. The full results are in detector-results.json.

The design question worth asking of any detector suite: does it check that the dependency ran, or just that the output looked right? The first can't be satisfied by accident. The second can — and that's where silent failures hide.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (FT-15, 226 scenarios)
  • Detector results: detector-results.json

articles.title: Your agent's retry bug isn't an AI problem. It's a distributed-systems problem with an LLM on top.
articles.description: Most agent demos have a happy path: the model picks a tool, the tool returns 200, the agent moves on....
articles.body_html:
Most agent demos have a happy path: the model picks a tool, the tool returns 200, the agent moves on. Production is different. In production, the tool call sometimes returns nothing at all.

That is where a correct decision turns into a wrong outcome.

The gap between "decided" and "done"

Here is an illustrative scenario (not a real incident, but a very ordinary one).

An agent handles a support ticket and decides the customer is owed a refund. It calls POST /refunds. The payments service processes the refund, writes it to its ledger, and starts sending the response. The network hiccups. The agent's HTTP client hits its timeout and raises an error.

From the agent's point of view, the call failed. From the payment service's point of view, it succeeded. The agent's loop sees an error, and the most natural thing for it to do is try again.

Now the customer has two refunds.

The model reasoned perfectly. It picked the right action with the right arguments. Nothing about better prompting, a bigger model, or a smarter planner fixes this, because the failure happened after the reasoning was over.

Failure mode 1: treating a timeout as a "no"

A timeout tells you one thing: you didn't get an answer. It does not tell you the action didn't happen. Agent frameworks that wrap tool errors into "the tool failed, decide what to do next" collapse three different situations into one:

  • the request never reached the service
  • the request reached it and was rejected
  • the request reached it, succeeded, and the response was lost

Only the first two are safe to retry blindly.

Failure mode 2: no idempotency key

If the agent had sent an idempotency key, the second refund call would have been a no-op that returned the original result. The key has to be generated by the application before the first attempt and reused on every retry of that same intent:

intent = actions.record_intent(
    kind="refund",
    order_id=order.id,
    amount=amount,
    idempotency_key=uuid4(),   # created once, stored with the intent
)

try:
    result = payments.refund(
        order_id=order.id,
        amount=amount,
        idempotency_key=intent.idempotency_key,
    )
    actions.mark_confirmed(intent.id, result)
except Timeout:
    actions.mark_unknown(intent.id)   # NOT "failed"

The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing.

Failure mode 3: state that only exists in the context window

If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The intent needs to be written to durable storage before execution, so that whatever process picks the work back up can see it.

Failure mode 4: no "outcome unknown" state

Most action models have two terminal states: success and failure. Reliable ones need at least:

  • submitted: we sent it, no answer yet
  • confirmed: the downstream system acknowledged it
  • failed: the downstream system explicitly rejected it
  • unknown: we can't tell

unknown is the one that matters. It's the state that should block automatic retries and trigger reconciliation instead.

Failure mode 5: no reconciliation path

When an action lands in unknown, something has to go find out the truth: query the payment service by idempotency key or order ID, compare against the ledger, and then move the intent to confirmed or failed. That can be a background job, a scheduled check, or a human queue for high-value actions. What it can't be is the agent deciding "probably fine" or "probably failed" on its own.

The reframe

Agent tool use is really remote procedure calls with an LLM choosing which procedure to call. Everything we already know about RPCs over unreliable networks still applies: idempotency, durable intent logs, explicit uncertainty, reconciliation.

The clean split is:

  • The model proposes an action.
  • The application owns the execution state: the key, the intent record, the status, the retry policy.

"Try again" is a fine default for reads. For anything that changes state, it's only safe once you know the first attempt didn't land, or once the downstream system guarantees a retry can't double-apply.

Build vs. integrate

If you already run payment or order flows with idempotency keys and outbox/ledger patterns, you mostly need to route agent actions through that same machinery instead of letting the agent call APIs directly. If you don't, that's the piece to build (or adopt) first, before giving an agent write access to anything that moves money or data.

How are you handling the "we don't know if it happened" case in your agent workflows? Are you blocking retries, reconciling, or escalating to a human?

articles.title: HisabMate: A Local-First, AI-Assisted Digital Bahi-Khata for Indian Microbusinesses
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

HisabMate is a local-first, AI-assisted bahi-khata (the traditional credit ledger) for Indian microbusinesses.

If you have ever bought something from a neighbourhood kirana, a tailor, or a small wholesaler, you have probably seen the system: a notebook where the owner writes who owes what. Customers take goods on credit (udhaar), pay back in pieces, and the owner reconciles it all by hand. It works because it is simple, but it is also fragile. Pages get smudged, entries go missing, and a disputed balance turns into an argument between two people who both want to stay on good terms.

Many bookkeeping tools exist, but they often assume cloud accounts, subscriptions, and a comfort with accounting vocabulary that a busy shopkeeper may not have. HisabMate takes a narrower path: keep the ledger on the owner's own machine, make the arithmetic exact and boring, and let a local language model help with the typing, never with the money.

The person who would pay for something like this is the owner who already runs on credit and handwritten pages and wants a clearer, searchable, exportable record without handing customer data to a third party. To be upfront: I have not had a paying user yet, so that is my hypothesis about the market, not a result.

Demo

HisabMate is not deployed publicly. It runs locally, and the two screenshots below are from the real application running on localhost.

Screenshot 1: HisabMate running locally at http://127.0.0.1:5174/.

Screenshot 2: a second view of the working local application.

Code

sm4006 / HisabMate

HisabMate

HisabMate is a local-first AI-assisted bahi-khata for Indian microbusinesses The Python backend owns validation, integer-paise calculations, SQLite persistence, idempotency, and CSV export. The React frontend is a local dashboard and review workflow.

Requirements

  • Python 3.10+ (Python 3.13+ is the target documented in the PRD)
  • Node.js and npm
  • Optional: Ollama for natural-language transaction proposals

No Python package installation is required: the backend uses the standard library. Frontend dependencies are declared in frontend/package.json.

Installation

From the repository root:

Set-Location .\frontend
npm install
Set-Location ..

The backend creates the SQLite schema automatically on first start. It does not seed customers or transactions.

Ollama setup

Install Ollama separately, start its local service, and install the configured model:

ollama pull llama3.2:3b

HisabMate uses llama3.2:3b by default through http://localhost:11434. Override the model or endpoint when needed:

$env:OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.2:3b"
$env:OLLAMA_HOST = "http://localhost:11434"

The…

View on GitHub

Repository: github.com/sm4006/HisabMate

How I Built It

Architecture

The design rule is that the model proposes and the code decides.

  • Backend (Python, standard library only). It owns validation, integer-paise calculations, SQLite persistence, idempotency, and CSV export. There are no Python packages to install.
  • Frontend (React). A local dashboard and review workflow that talks to the backend API at http://127.0.0.1:8000/api.
  • AI layer (Ollama). HisabMate uses llama3.2:3b by default through a local Ollama service at http://localhost:11434. The model and endpoint can be overridden with the OLLAMA_MODEL and OLLAMA_HOST environment variables.
  • Storage. A local SQLite database. The schema is created automatically on first start, and nothing is seeded.

Safeguards documented in the repository

Money software has to be dull in the right places, so these are the parts I care about most:

  • Integer paise, never floats. Credit and payment amounts are stored as integer paise, with exact two-decimal rupee/paise input validation. Balances are deterministic.
  • Model output is a proposal only. When Ollama interprets a natural-language entry, the response goes through strict validation in Python. Nothing is written to the ledger until the user explicitly confirms it.
  • Idempotent confirmations. Confirmed transaction submissions use persistent idempotency, so a double click or a retry does not create a duplicate entry.
  • Append-only corrections. Mistakes are corrected by adding a new entry with an audit reference, not by silently editing history, much like striking through a line in a paper ledger.
  • Safer CSV export. Text fields that begin with spreadsheet formula characters are escaped, so an exported file does not turn a customer name into a formula.
  • Honest empty fields. The CSV has a remarks column, but the current schema stores no remarks, so it is exported blank rather than guessed.

What works today

  • Customer records with outstanding balances calculated from the ledger.
  • Credit and payment transactions.
  • Local Ollama transaction proposals with an explicit confirmation step.
  • Customer-specific ledgers and a Daily Hisab view filtered by business date, customer, transaction type, and search text.
  • Transaction-history CSV export that respects the active filters.
  • Loading, empty, validation, offline, and API-error states in the frontend.
  • A Python unittest suite, a compile check, and a frontend build, all runnable from the README commands.

How GitHub Copilot fits in

I used GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code, primarily in Agent mode, as a coding assistant throughout HisabMate's development.

I used it to help implement and refine the Python ledger and API, build the React/Vite interface, develop the AI-assisted transaction proposal flow, add Daily Hisab filters and CSV export, and expand tests and project documentation. I worked incrementally, reviewing the implementation and testing the application between tasks.

One concrete moment where it helped: Copilot helped connect the customer-specific ledger view to the backend so that selecting a customer displayed that customer's transactions and outstanding balance rather than generic or unrelated data.

One moment that required correction: During the final submission process, I had to correct the Git remote configuration before the existing local commit could be pushed to GitHub. This was a reminder that agent-generated instructions still need to be checked against the actual repository state.

What remained human-owned: The core financial-safety decisions were not delegated to the model. Transaction amounts use integer paise, the backend validates proposed transactions, and the user must review and explicitly confirm a transaction before it is written to the ledger. The AI proposes an interpretation; it does not get direct database-write authority.

I also reviewed the generated changes, ran tests and build checks, and checked the application against the intended workflow rather than treating generated code as automatically correct.

Repository: https://github.com/sm4006/HisabMate

Copilot was a development aid, not a substitute for reviewing financial logic or verifying the finished application.

Known Limitations

I would rather list these here than have a reader discover them:

  • No contact details or opening balances. The current SQLite schema does not represent them.
  • No free-text remarks. They are not stored, so search covers customer names and controlled transaction labels only.
  • Out of scope for this release: payment reminders, CSV customization, bank integrations, and multi-user accounts.
  • No frontend unit or end-to-end test framework. The browser workflows were manually exercised against disposable local services, and the Python suite is the automated safety net.
  • Ollama must be installed and running for live interpretation. The normal Python test suite does not need it.
  • A 3B model is small. I am not publishing accuracy benchmarks for its interpretations. That is exactly why every proposal needs a human confirmation before it touches the ledger.
  • Setup instructions in the README use PowerShell syntax. Other shells will need small adjustments.
  • Not deployed. There is no hosted version. It is meant to run on the owner's own machine.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a small business, a ledger is not just data. It is who trusts whom, and how much. Open-weight models and local inference change what is possible here:

  1. The data can stay on the owner's machine. By default, HisabMate points at a local Ollama endpoint and a local SQLite file. A closed hosted API would mean sending customer names and amounts to a server the shopkeeper does not control.
  2. The cost model fits the customer. A microbusiness cannot easily absorb per-request fees or a monthly subscription for something that used to be a notebook. Running a model locally has no per-call bill.
  3. The model is swappable. Because the model name and host are configuration, not a vendor contract, the owner or a local developer can try a different open model without rewriting the application.
  4. The behaviour is inspectable. The backend is plain Python and the rules that guard the money are readable. For software that tracks who owes whom, being able to read the rules is a feature.

The honest trade-off is capability. A small local model is weaker than a large hosted one, which is why HisabMate treats it as a typing assistant behind a validation boundary rather than as an authority.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot

Thanks for reading, and for any feedback, especially from anyone who has run a credit-based shop and knows what a real bahi-khata needs.

articles.description: After 10 years of working as a software engineer in web development, I joined a company in the energy...
articles.body_html:
After 10 years of working as a software engineer in web development, I joined a company in the energy industry. To be precise, in solutions for the power grid.

I thought that the new domain would be the hardest and biggest challenge. And it was really very hard to understand such a complex industry, both from a regulatory and a technical perspective. It took me 6 months to finally build a mental map in my head. The result of my inquiries was this series: A Developer’s Map of the European Power Grid.

When I went deeper into developing and designing software systems for the field, I faced another unexpected problem. Let me first give you some context to understand the problem better.

The grid is a complex... no... COMPLEX graph of interconnected logical nodes. It is a complicated network of networks. And in most cases, when you build something for the grid, you end up reconstructing its structure in software and networks. Either as part of a solution or as an environment for testing and simulation.

The grid is a live structure that heavily depends on communication between its nodes. It is the most important property of the grid. And to fulfill its communication needs, there are a lot of different protocols, standards, and requirements. And you have to be VERY precise with them and understand their internals very deeply.

In web development, the lowest-level communication I had to deal with was constructing the headers of an HTTP request. In the energy industry, you need to construct multicast messages byte by byte and send them at a specific time over a network with a strictly defined topology and nanosecond precision.

And here an unexpected problem popped up: I, a web dev with a decade of experience, did not know networking. At least not at the level needed for such manipulations.

I jumped into it: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach by James Kurose, then Beej's Guide to Networking Concepts, then Computer Networking Fundamentals for Developers, DevOps, and Platform Engineers, and finally Linux Kernel Networking: Implementation and Theory by Rami Rosen.

A few months of reading, building, trying, writing, and chatting with ChatGPT, and here is the result of my work:
Networking Machinery for Software Engineers

Everything that you might need to know as a software engineer to feel comfortable with any networking topic.

It was created with the energy industry in mind, but it will be useful for any developer.

Of course, it doesn't mean that I know everything about networking now. Quite the opposite. But at least I finally have a solid foundation and a mental map that helps me understand how all these pieces work together.

I hope this series will help other developers who find themselves in a similar situation, or who simply want to understand what is happening underneath their applications.

And here is my request to you:
Take a look at the series and tell me what you think! Did I miss something important? Is something unclear or technically incorrect? Or maybe there is a topic you think deserves more attention?

I would really appreciate your feedback, especially from people who work with networking every day.
