articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

My neighbours run a grocery shop. Like thousands of small shops, they sell a lot on credit and keep track in a khata: a paper ledger where every row is a customer, a date, an item, and either udhar (the customer took goods on credit) or jama (they paid something back).
It works until you need an answer. Who owes what? Who hasn't paid in over a month? The answer is somewhere in the pages, and finding it means turning them over by hand.

So I built Ledgerly. You photograph a page. A vision model reads every row. You get a review screen with your photo beside the extracted rows, fix whatever it got wrong, confirm, and the app keeps running balances per customer, with an aging report: who is over 30 days.

The part I care about most is the loop. Every page you confirm carries your corrections, and those corrections are the training data for the next fine-tune (python ft/train.py --from-db). Using the app produces training data.

It reads Hindi (Devanagari), English, and the mixed pages that real ledgers actually are.

Demo

The demo covers gemma running locally and extracting entries from a handwritten ledger page and other functionalities of Ledgerly web app.

What my neighbours said

I asked my neighbours to try it. They found the screens easy to understand almost immediately: the photo next to the rows, the big buttons, the "owes money" and "over 30 days" filters. Their own khata is laid out differently from the pages I trained on, so they couldn't run their book through it yet. They told me they would definitely use it if I rolled it out as an app.

That told me what to build next. The model has to learn their page, and that is what fine-tuning is for: photograph a few pages, label them, and train again for about forty cents.

The side hustle

Who would pay: small shops that sell on credit and still run their books on paper, like my neighbours. They don't need another accounting suite. They need to stop turning pages to find out who owes what.

What I'd sell: the model and the pipeline are open and stay free. I'd charge for the convenience: a hosted version where the shopkeeper photographs a page and the ledger is ready, plus the part that matters most, teaching the model that shop's own page layout. My neighbours' khata looks different from mine, so a one-time setup is exactly what they need: a few photographed and labelled pages, then a fine-tune. The compute for my 9-page run cost about forty cents.

Pricing:: I asked my neighbours what would feel fair for an app like this, and they said ₹100 to ₹150 a month. So I'd offer a free tier of about 20 pages a month, so a shop can try it on its own khata, then roughly ₹120-₹130 a month per shop. A one-time setup would teach the model that shop's own page layout. That's a few rupees a day, far less than the hours lost to the paper book, and in line with what small shops already pay for billing apps.

The price comes from one shop's answer and the idea hasn't been tested beyond that, but they told me they would use it.

Code

arkia09 / Ledgerly

Ledgerly

Photograph a page of a paper credit ledger. A local Gemma model (via Ollama) reads it, you correct mistakes, and the app reports who owes what and for how long.

Layout

  • extraction/ Step 1: model prompt, schema, single/batch runners, scoring
  • backend/ Step 2: Django API (SQLite, no login)
  • frontend/ Step 3: React + TypeScript app (Vite)
  • finetune/ Optional: fine-tune a vision model on Tinker and compare with the baseline (see its README)
  • data/pages/ test photos (gitignored: may contain customer data)
  • data/ground_truth/ your hand-written correct answers, one JSON per photo
  • data/outputs/ model outputs per run (gitignored)

Setup (Windows PowerShell)

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
ollama pull gemma4:e4b

Step 1 workflow

  1. Put photos in data/pages/ (page01.jpg, page02.jpg, ...).
  2. For each, copy data/ground_truth/_template.json to page01.json and fill in the true rows Set "page_type" to neat, messy or mixed.
  3. Edit the layout line in extraction/prompt.txt to match your ledger.
  4. …
View on GitHub

Django + SQLite backend, React + TypeScript frontend, and an extraction/ft/ folder that holds the whole fine-tuning pipeline: dataset.py, train.py, sampler.py, evaluate.py, compare.py.

How I Built It 

photo ──▶ preprocess
      ──▶ vision model ──▶ JSON { rows: [ {date, name, item, amount, type, struck_out} ] }
      ──▶ pydantic schema check
      ──▶ review screen (you fix rows) ──▶ confirm ──▶ ledger + aging report
                                                │
                    corrections ◀───────────────┘  (next training run, --from-db)

Each row has exactly six fields. type is credit (udhar) or payment (jama), and struck_out is true when the shopkeeper has crossed a row out, so it is stored but not counted:

{ "date": "15/10", "name": "Ramesh Kumar", "item": "Atta (5 kg)",
  "amount": 240, "type": "credit", "struck_out": false }

Step 1: the baseline, with a local Gemma

The first version ran Gemma 4 e4b locally through Ollama. Nothing leaves the computer, which matters for a book full of customers' names and debts. It works, but it takes about 159 seconds per page on my CPU.

Step 2: the data (the boring part that decides everything)

I labelled 14 pages by hand (took me 2 hours), one JSON of ground truth per photo. Then I split them so the model is judged on pages it has never seen:

  • Held out (5 pages, 50 rows): page02, page04, page06 (my original neat, messy and mixed pages) plus page09 and page10.
  • Trained on (9 pages): the rest.

I picked page09 and page10 as test pages on purpose. Several of my new pages repeat each other's customers and amounts (page 8 and page 14 are nearly identical). If a test page has a twin in training, the score is inflated. Those two had no twins.

Nine pages is tiny, so dataset.py adds three augmented copies of each page (small rotation, brightness, contrast and crop). That makes 36 training examples, 79,764 tokens per epoch.

Step 3: fine-tuning on Tinker

Choosing the model

The input is a photograph, so I needed a vision model. My first choice, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, died on the first real run with 400: base_model ... is not supported. The public docs still listed it. So I asked the server what my key could use (ServiceClient().get_server_capabilities()), and the list had moved on to Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6, plus Nemotron and others.

I picked Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: a mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active parameters, which keeps training and sampling cheap, in the same size class as the model I'd planned. A free --dry-run rendered every example with the real tokenizer and image processor before I spent anything, and the renderer it chose (qwen3_5) matched what tinker_cookbook recommends for that model.

I used Tinker to LoRA fine-tune it with the settings in train.py:

Setting Value
Method LoRA, rank 16
Epochs / batch size 4 / 4, so 36 steps
Learning rate 1e-4, decaying to 1e-5
Renderer qwen3_5 (matches get_recommended_renderer_name)
Training cost about $0.38 of credit ($10.00 to $9.62)

Every example is a (photo, correct JSON) pair.

epoch 1/4 step 1/36  loss/token 0.1466
epoch 1/4 step 9/36  loss/token 0.0185
epoch 2/4 step 18/36 loss/token 0.0050
epoch 3/4 step 27/36 loss/token 0.0013
epoch 4/4 step 36/36 loss/token 0.0008

I'm not treating that curve as a result. It's loss on training pages the model saw four times each, so it says the run was healthy, not that the model is good.

Step 4: the evaluation

ft/evaluate.py runs the untouched base model and the fine-tuned model on the five held-out pages and scores both with my own score.py. Each true row has to be matched to a predicted row, and then name, amount, date, type and crossed-out flag are checked. A row counts as "full" only when all five are right.

The base model scored 0%. I want to be precise about why. It did not read the pages badly. On all five pages it failed to produce valid JSON for my schema (wrong shape, no JSON object at all, or text after the JSON). score.py can only score what it can parse, so every page became "found 0 rows". That number measures instruction-following on one schema, not handwriting, so I'm not using it as my "before". Gemma is my baseline, because it produces valid output.

Fine-tuned Qwen against local Gemma, 50 rows, same pages, same checker:

Gemma 4 e4b (local) Qwen3.6 fine-tuned (Tinker)
Full row correct 41/50 (82%) 44/50 (88%)
Name 46/50 45/50
Amount 48/50 49/50
Date 47/50 49/50
Type (credit vs payment) 44/50 (88%) 49/50 (98%)
Crossed out 47/50 48/50
Extra rows invented 0 0
Seconds per page 159 s (laptop CPU) 12 s (Tinker cloud GPU)

Fully right rows by kind of page (this is the part I'd look at before trusting any single percentage):

Page type Rows Gemma 4 e4b (local) Qwen3.6 fine-tuned
Neat (page02, page09, page10) 30 26 (87%) 28 (93%)
Messy (page04) 10 7 (70%) 10 (100%)
Mixed Hindi/English (page06) 10 8 (80%) 6 (60%)

What stands out:

  1. Credit versus payment went from 88% to 98%. In a ledger that is the field that matters most: mixing up udhar and jama flips the sign on someone's balance.
  2. Three more rows fully right out of 50 (82% to 88%), with dates, amounts and crossed-out flags all a little better and no invented rows.
  3. 12 seconds a page instead of 159. That compares a cloud GPU with my laptop CPU, so read it as "hosted versus on my machine", not as a model-size result.
  4. Where it's level or behind: names (45 against Gemma's 46) and my one mixed Hindi/English page (6 of 10 rows against 8). On the neat and messy pages it got 28 of 30 and 10 of 10 rows fully right.

With 50 test rows, a one or two row gap is noise, so I trust the type and speed results most.

Two details from walking through every row in compare.html:

  • One label was my mistake. On page06, row 7, my ground-truth JSON said the row was crossed out, but I never crossed it out on the paper. Both models said "not crossed out", so both were marked wrong for being right. I corrected that one label after seeing the results and rescored both models, so the numbers above include the fix.
  • One real miss: the fine-tuned model wrote "Pooja" in Latin letters where the ledger has the name in Devanagari. It's the same person, but the tool is meant to copy what's written, so I left it counted as wrong. Several of the other name misses were rows Gemma read correctly.

Step 5: seeing the mistakes, not just the percentages

ft/compare.py builds one HTML page: my photo, my ground truth, and every model side by side, with wrong fields in red and the correct value underneath. I used it to find that the mixed page was where the fine-tuned model lost rows.

Using it in the app

One environment variable decides who reads the page:

$env:LEDGERLY_EXTRACTOR = "tinker"   # default is the local Gemma via Ollama

The default keeps every photo on the computer. With tinker, each photo is sent to Tinker's cloud to be read by the fine-tuned model, and the README says so. The API key lives in an environment variable and nowhere in the repo.

What I got wrong on the way

  • I almost trained on three pages. I had put all eight new pages into the held-out list. That left the training set exactly where it started. Reading the dry-run's "36 examples" line is what caught the mistake.

  • My new photos were .jpeg, and the pipeline looked for .jpg. They were skipped without a single warning. Renaming fixed it.

    What I learned

  • Label quality matters as much as quantity. Some of the mistakes I found in compare.html were mine, not the model's: a "crossed out" label on a row I never crossed out. A model can only be as consistent as the labels it is trained and judged on.

  • Measure the baseline fairly. Base Qwen's 0% looked dramatic and meant "can't follow my JSON format". Gemma was the honest comparison.

  • Look at the rows, not just the percentages. The scoreboard said the fine-tuned model was a little better. The side-by-side page showed where: credit versus payment and the neat and messy pages, not the mixed one.

  • Dry-run first. The whole fine-tune cost about forty cents because I rendered everything for free before spending any credit.

What's next

  • Learn the neighbours' khata. Label a few pages in their layout and run the same pipeline. Every page they confirm in the app becomes training data (--from-db).
  • More writers. My own handwriting is in all 14 pages. Pages from other hands will show how far the model carries.
  • Publish the adapter on Hugging Face (Tinker can push a checkpoint straight there), so anyone can run it on their own hardware.
  • Package it as an app so a shopkeeper can use it without a laptop.

The review screen is part of the design: the model proposes the rows, the shopkeeper confirms them, and nothing reaches the ledger unchecked.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • It stays on the shopkeeper's computer. A khata is a list of who owes whom. With open weights the default path never uploads a photo, and the cloud path is opt-in and said out loud.
  • I could change the model and measure it. Tinker let me fine-tune open weights for about 38 cents, and I could run that against an open baseline on the same pages with the same scorer. Swapping the base model is one variable (TINKER_BASE_MODEL).
  • I could see why it was wrong. The comparison page shows each wrong field next to the right value, so I could tell a reading error from a spelling variant instead of trusting one score.

  • The result is reproducible. Open weights, my labelled pages, my scorer and the saved outputs are all in the repo, so anyone can rerun the comparison.

    Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Tinker: LoRA fine-tune of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 36 augmented examples, scored on 5 held-out pages against a local baseline, for about $0.38.

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 e4b runs locally through Ollama as the private default and as the baseline the fine-tuned model has to beat.

Built with Claude and tea ☕.

articles.title: Exact-Match Edits vs Patches: How Claude Code, Codex and Aider Write to Your Files
articles.description: Claude Code's Edit refuses a duplicate match; Codex's apply_patch and Aider's SEARCH/REPLACE take the first one. How each edit protocol fails.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your config file has two functions that both set timeout = 30. You ask a coding agent to raise the production timeout to 60. Depending on which agent you asked, one of two things happens. The edit is refused until the agent adds more context. Or the first timeout = 30 in the file changes, which is the development one, and the patch applies cleanly.

The edit protocol decides that outcome: the format the agent uses to describe a change, and the code on your machine that applies it. Claude Code, Codex and Aider each use a different one, and their docs and source say exactly what happens when the text doesn't line up.

Here is the file used for every case below:

def load_dev():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 3

def load_prod():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 5

Three ways to say "change this line"

Claude Code: exact string replacement. The Edit tool takes an old_string and a new_string and, in the docs' words, "doesn't use regex or fuzzy matching." Three checks must pass: Claude has read the file, old_string appears exactly as written, and it appears exactly once unless replace_all: true is set. The read rule is looser for newer models. The same page says Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5 and older models always require the read, while newer models on Claude Code v2.1.208 or later can skip it when the Read tool is available and reading wouldn't need a permission prompt.

The documented fields, for our task:

Edit
  old_string: "    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex: patch envelopes. OpenAI's Codex Prompting Guide tells you to use apply_patch for single-file edits, says the model "has been trained to excel at this diff format", and strongly recommends using OpenAI's exact implementation. That implementation is open source in the codex-rs/apply-patch crate. Its markers are *** Begin Patch, *** Add File:, *** Delete File:, *** Update File:, *** Move to:, *** End of File, @@ and *** End Patch. Changed lines start with - or +, context lines with a space, and there are no line numbers:

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider: you pick the format. Aider's edit formats include whole (the model returns the entire file), diff (SEARCH/REPLACE blocks), diff-fenced (the same blocks with the path inside the fence, mainly for Gemini models), udiff (a simplified unified diff) and two editor- variants for architect mode. A diff block looks like a merge conflict:

config.py
```python
<<<<<<< SEARCH
    timeout = 30
=======
    timeout = 60
>>>>>>> REPLACE
```

Aider also publishes how often models get the format right. Its polyglot leaderboard, last updated November 20, 2025, puts a "Correct edit format" column next to the pass rate over 225 exercises. gpt-5 (high) tops the table at 88.0% correct, with 91.6% on edit format using diff. Even the top model sent a malformed edit in some cases, and the applier has to catch each one.

The duplicate line: one refuses, two pick the first

Claude Code's uniqueness check fails, because timeout = 30 appears twice. Per the docs, Claude then "either supplies a longer string with enough surrounding context to pin down one occurrence, or sets replace_all: true to replace them all." The retry that works carries the function header:

Edit
  old_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex's applier doesn't check uniqueness. In file_update.rs, each chunk's old lines are searched from the current position forward, and seek_sequence.rs returns the first window that matches without looking at later ones. With the bare @@ patch above, the first timeout = 30 sits in load_dev. That line changes.

The anchor fixes it. Text after @@ is a change context: the applier finds that line first and only searches for the old lines after it.

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@ def load_prod():
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider's diff format behaves like Codex here. In editblock_coder.py, perfect_replace replaces the first block of lines that matches and returns. One path is stricter. When a SEARCH block uses ... to elide lines, Aider refuses the block if that chunk appears more than once.

To be fair to Codex and Aider, models rarely send one bare line. Context lines in a patch and a multi-line SEARCH block usually make the match unique anyway. The difference shows up when they don't: Claude Code stops, the other two apply at the first match.

Stale context: the file moved since the model looked

The model's copy of a file goes stale when you edit it, a formatter runs, or a second agent touches it.

Claude Code has a documented rule for this case. Since v2.1.208, if the file changed after Claude's last read but old_string still matches the current content "exactly and unambiguously" and the file is readable without a prompt, the edit applies and the result notes that the file carries other changes, so Claude re-reads before edits that depend on the surrounding code. In any other case, such as a stale old_string, Claude reads the file again before editing. Before v2.1.208 it refused any edit to a file that changed on disk after the read.

Codex fails with a message the model can act on. If the @@ line isn't found, file_update.rs returns Failed to find context '<line>' in <path>. If the old lines aren't found, it returns Failed to find expected lines in <path>: followed by the lines it looked for. The API guide describes the same loop for your own harness: report status: "failed" with a short human-readable message.

Aider replies with SearchReplaceNoExactMatch: This SEARCH block failed to exactly match lines in <path>, plus the reminder that "The SEARCH section must exactly match an existing block of lines including all white space, comments, indentation, docstrings, etc". If misses keep coming, its troubleshooting page suggests, among other things, --edit-format whole.

The whole format can't miss a match, because there is nothing to match. If the model's copy of the file was old, though, the rewrite puts that old version back over whatever changed since, and nothing reports an error. The other risk is elision. The edit-formats page says udiff was mainly used with GPT-4 Turbo because it reduced that model's habit of eliding code with comments like "original code here". In Aider's unified diffs write-up, moving GPT-4 Turbo from SEARCH/REPLACE to udiff raised its laziness benchmark score from 20% to 61%.

Whitespace drift: strict, forgiving, and in between

Models re-type the text they want to replace, and re-typing drifts. A tab comes back as four spaces, trailing whitespace disappears, a straight quote turns curly.

Claude Code is strict on purpose. The docs say "A single character of whitespace or indentation difference is enough to miss." When it misses, the edit doesn't apply.

Codex's applier is the most forgiving of the three. seek_sequence makes four passes in what its comment calls "decreasing strictness": an exact match, then ignoring trailing whitespace, then trimming both sides, then normalising common Unicode punctuation like dashes and quotes to ASCII. Indentation drift in the old lines still finds its target. The price shows up when nothing matches exactly. A looser pass can match in more places, and the first window it finds wins.

Aider sits in between. It tries an exact match, then a match that tolerates missing leading whitespace, then retries without a stray blank first line. A fuzzy edit-distance matcher exists in the same file, but a bare return sits in front of the call, so it never runs.

Leniency pays off. The same unified diffs write-up reports that turning flexible patching off produced "a 9X increase in editing errors".

Failure Claude Code Edit Codex apply_patch Aider diff
Duplicate match Refused First match after anchor First match
Stale text Applies if still exact, else re-reads Error to model Error to model
Whitespace drift Miss Four lenient passes Tolerates leading whitespace

An undo that doesn't care how the bytes got there

Every failure above has a quiet version: the edit applies in the wrong place, or on top of stale assumptions, and the agent reports success. You catch it in review, and then you want that one turn back.

Each tool has its own answer. Claude Code's checkpoints capture your code before each prompt, and /rewind restores code, conversation or both. The docs are clear about the edge: "Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands", and most subagent edits aren't restored either. Aider commits every edit to git with a descriptive message, and /undo discards the last change. Each one covers its own agent's edits and nothing else.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this with that in mind. Hermes runs Claude Code, Codex, Aider and other agents, each in its own terminal, and saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore any single turn, with undo (README). The strip under a session lists the agent's replies with the lines each changed. Click one to see its changes or restore your files to that point (2.3.1 notes). The Review Desk (⌘G) shows the same work by turn or by file.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view for a Claude Code task: two turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

Because the snapshot is of your files, not of the edit calls, the same restore works for every agent, whether the change arrived as an old_string, a patch envelope or a SEARCH block. There are two limits. In a Claude Code task with extra folders, the strip tracks the main project only (2.3.1 notes). Turn snapshots from tasks that ran in their own worktree are removed 14 days after the session closes (2.2.9 notes).

What to do with this

If you run Codex or Aider on files with repeated blocks, like per-environment config or test tables, check where the diff landed, not only what it says.

If Claude Code keeps missing an edit, look for mixed tabs and spaces or invisible characters in the file before you blame the model. If you use Aider's whole format, keep other writers off that file while the agent works, because a rewrite from a stale copy applies without an error.

Whatever the protocol, keep a per-turn record outside the edit path: plain commits, Aider's auto-commit, or a turn snapshot.

If this was useful

An edit format is structured output with a strict parser on the other end, and Aider's leaderboard shows that even top models miss the format in some share of cases. If you write prompts that ask a model for output a program has to parse, the Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide is my short book on prompting techniques, structured output among them. If you run several of these agents side by side, Hermes IDE is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and lives on GitHub.

articles.title: Someone built a programming language to break LLMs. I ran it.
articles.description: KillSwitch is an esolang designed to be unusable by LLMs: a lying spec, anagram-only function calls, values chosen by dice roll. I built its interpreter, ran every sample program, diffed its two specs (484 lines vs 887,584 words of decoy), and found its CLI test suite fails 10/10 on a fresh clone for a naming bug.
articles.body_html:
Dominik Picheta built a programming language whose design goal is to be unusable by LLMs. It's called KillSwitch, it hit Hacker News yesterday, and the pitch is specific: the spec contains lies, identifiers are referenced by anagram, function calls are phrased as jailbreak bait, and values are counted in letters. He also published a benchmark: the best model so far scores 66.8 out of 100 on tasks like "implement hello world" and "invert a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit converter."

I cloned the repo, built the interpreter, and ran everything in it. Here's what the numbers look like from the inside.

The two specs

The repo ships two specification documents. They are not the same size.

SPEC.md      484 lines     2,773 words
AI_SPEC.md   65,495 lines  887,584 words

AI_SPEC.md is 320x the words of the real spec. So I counted what is actually in it:

occurrences in AI_SPEC.md (65,495 lines):
  "KillSwitch"   0
  "stack"        0
  "adverb"       0
  markdown headings   0
  unique lines   19,695 of 65,495  (70% are repeats)

It is filler — long stretches of literary criticism and stage-direction-like fragments, committed under the message "Enhance the AI spec." An agent that dutifully loads both documents spends roughly 1.2 million tokens of context on a file that never once names the language it supposedly specifies. The real spec is 484 lines. The decoy is the attack.

Running the examples

The interpreter is a 2.2 MB Rust binary. It builds cleanly, and the sample programs work — once you notice that several of them read stdin, and that feeding them EOF produces the least helpful error in the repo:

$ killswitch run tests/fahrenheit.ks < /dev/null
Error: Couldn't parse ''

$ printf "23\n" | killswitch run tests/fahrenheit.ks
73.4

With input supplied, everything checks out:

fahrenheit   23 C      ->  73.4
factorial    11        ->  39916800
max          2, 78847  ->  78847
max          -78847, 2 ->  2
greeting     Alice, 32 ->  Hello Alice, your age is 32
fizzbuzz     1..20     ->  1 2 fizz 4 buzz ... fizzbuzz (correct)
promo                  ->  Hello World

The anagram rule is real, and it bites

Built-in operations cannot be called by their actual names. A program that tries gets rejected at runtime:

$ killswitch run tests/error_multiply.ks
Error: Invalid func call, need an anagram of multiply

The CLI ships a helper for this — its help text describes it as "Only useful for LLMs," which is fair. I generated an anagram by hand and checked it:

$ killswitch anagram multiply lumpytil
multiply is an anagram of lumpytil

lumpytil is not a word. The spec says the interpreter prefers it that way: call sites must use an anagram of the definition's name, and nonsense anagrams make it happiest. Every function call in every sample program works like this, which means a model writing KillSwitch has to do exact letter-multiset arithmetic on every single call — the one operation LLMs are famously sloppy at — with zero tolerance.

The second trap I tripped on myself: when a sentence contains more than one candidate value, the interpreter picks one at random and warns you:

[W102] Warning: Possible gotcha
  Value deduced was chosen at random

That was greeting.ks, printing Hello , your age is with the name missing, because the value it grabbed was chosen by dice roll. Deterministic languages are hard enough for models. This one has a dice cup in the value-resolution path.

The test suite disagrees with itself 

$ cargo test --release
unit tests:   70 passed, 0 failed
CLI tests:    0 passed, 10 failed

All ten CLI tests fail on a fresh clone — not because the binary is broken (I ran the exact cases they assert, above, and they pass), but because of a naming mismatch: the package is killswitch-lang, the binary is killswitch, and the test harness looks up the binary by package name:

thread 'test_cli_promo' panicked:
  `CARGO_BIN_EXE_killswitch-lang` is unset
  help: available binary names are "killswitch"

A language designed to break automated tooling has a test suite that its own automated tooling can't run. I choose to believe this is a coincidence.

What this actually measures

The author's own framing is honest: a best score of 66.8 on simple tasks doesn't prove models "understand" the language, and failure wouldn't prove they don't understand code in general. What KillSwitch isolates is narrower and, I think, more useful. Strip away the guardrail bait and the decoy documents and the core difficulty is clerical: exact counting, exact letter inventories, line-number bookkeeping, and a spec that punishes skimming. Those are precisely the operations that token-based models approximate instead of compute.

Every coding agent I've used fails the same way KillSwitch wants it to fail — confidently, fluently, and off by one letter. Picheta just built the first benchmark where that's the whole test.

Sources: the author's post, the repo, the benchmark leaderboard. All outputs above are from the reference interpreter, v0.1.4, built and run locally.

articles.body_html:
HustlePilot: an AI copilot for small businesses that is not allowed to invent numbers

Draft DEV post for Hacktoberfest 2026. AI disclosure: this project and this draft were built with agent assistance (some_ai).

Small sellers — a plant nursery in this case — already have data: WhatsApp order notes, a sales CSV, a products sheet. What they don't have is time to read it every morning. HustlePilot is a local-first AI copilot that turns three CSVs into a ranked morning briefing: what's running low, what's slowing down, which inquiries went cold, and which listings are thin.

The interesting part isn't the LLM. It's the rules around it.

The one design rule: code computes, the LLM writes

Every number you see in HustlePilot — stock cover, sales rate ratios, days waiting on an inquiry — is computed by deterministic pandas rules (backend/app/services/analytics.py). The LLM's only job is to turn that evidence into a sentence a human would write.

And it may only reuse numbers that appear in the evidence. Before any narrative reaches the UI, a grounding validator (backend/app/services/grounding.py) extracts every number from the LLM's text and checks it against the evidence dict:

def safe_narrative(opp_type, evidence, llm_text, extra=None):
    """Return (narrative, source, rejected_numbers)."""
    if llm_text:
        bad = ungrounded_numbers(llm_text, evidence, extra)
        if not bad:
            return llm_text.strip(), "llm", []
        return TEMPLATES[opp_type], "template", sorted(bad)
    return TEMPLATES[opp_type], "template", []

If the model says "you sold 94 units last week" and the evidence says 14, the whole narrative is replaced with a boring-but-true template, the rejection is counted, and the UI labels the source (llm vs template). The model can't quietly delete a bad number — the entire text is forfeited. That's on purpose: partial edits are harder to audit than all-or-nothing fallback.

This mirrors a pattern the community keeps re-learning: search-enabled or retrieval-enabled LLMs still get numbers wrong, because retrieval fixes access to facts, not faithfulness in restating them (Why Search-Enabled LLMs Still Get Numbers Wrong 👤 @yany-henry). A validator at the output boundary is the part that actually enforces it (Why your AI agent keeps hallucinating financial data (and how to fix it) 👤 @valyuai).

Screenshots

Architecture in one screen

  • Backend: FastAPI + SQLite (single file, tenant-scoped rows with a business_id, demo API-key auth — it's a single-tenant demo, not multi-tenant SaaS).
  • LLM: any Ollama-compatible endpoint (gemma3:4b locally) or a deterministic mock. Every provider response is labeled real/mock in the UI. No GPU required; inference runs CPU-bound on a laptop.
  • Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind. Dashboard, CSV import with validation reports, opportunity feed, listing studio, inquiry inbox, approvals queue (draft → approved → exported), history timeline.
  • Eval harness (eval/run_eval.py): five stages — CSV-defect injection, a hand-computed rules fixture, grounding unit checks, labeled inquiry classification vs. a keyword baseline, and latency.

The approval queue matters more than it sounds. Generated drafts never send themselves: an inquiry reply or listing draft sits as submitted until the owner approves, edits, or dismisses it. Every state change is audited.

What the eval actually measured

Honest numbers, with sample sizes:

Stage Result
CSV validation, 30 injected defects 30/30 detected, 0 errors on clean files
Rules fixture (hand-computed expectations) 14/14 checks pass
Grounding unit checks 7/7 (fabricated numbers rejected, ratio edge cases, URL flagging)
Backend tests (pytest, mock providers) 35 passed
API smoke (end-to-end through HTTP) 36/36 checks pass
Real-model latency (gemma3:4b, CPU, n=1) analyze ≈ 77 s · listing ≈ 50 s · inquiry ≈ 56 s

What was not measured, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise: listing-copy quality has no human rating yet; classification accuracy against the labeled fixture is a small-n, single-domain test; and the before/after comparison view in the app is correlational — nothing in HustlePilot claims an action caused a sale. The rules carry honest limitations text on every opportunity for exactly this reason.

Small things that saved the demo

  • AS_OF is derived from max(sale_date), not today's clock — demos are reproducible, and "days waiting" doesn't drift between rehearsals.
  • Slow-mover analysis refuses to run with fewer than recent + baseline days of history (112 by default) and says so in a notice, instead of quietly computing nonsense on two weeks of data.
  • Mock everything, label everything. LLM_PROVIDER=mock and SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock make the full stack testable in CI, and the UI never lets a mock output masquerade as a real one.
  • >20% invalid rows rejects the whole CSV with an explanation, rather than importing the silent majority.

Run it 

# backend
cd backend && pip install -r requirements.txt
cp ../.env.example ../.env   # LLM_PROVIDER=ollama, SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock
uvicorn app.main:app --reload

# frontend
cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev   # proxies /api → :8000

# tests + eval
LLM_PROVIDER=mock SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock pytest -q
python eval/run_eval.py --stage validation --llm mock
python eval/run_eval.py --stage classification --llm real --limit 12

Hit Import sample data in the UI to load a fictional Bengaluru plant nursery (8 products, 619 sales, 5 inquiries).

TL;DR

An LLM that writes your morning briefing is a liability. An LLM that writes your morning briefing under a numeric grounding check, behind an approval queue, with every fallback visible in the UI is a tool. Code computes; the LLM narrates; the human decides.

Built for Hacktoberfest 2026. Feedback, PRs, and "you should have used X instead" all welcome.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

https://voice-order-taker-jvh7zuvem9z6qbfuqfcvpm.streamlit.app/

What I Built

Voice Order Taker is a local app that turns WhatsApp voice notes into a clean order sheet.

In Pakistan, a lot of home businesses run on voice notes. A baker, a tiffin cook or a small clothing seller gets messages like "do kilo chocolate cake aur teen dozen samosay kal shaam tak, house 12 Jinnah Road", in Urdu, Roman Urdu, Pashto or a mix with English. The seller replays each note, then writes the order down by hand. With 20 or more orders a week, that is hours of work, and one misheard quantity means a wrong delivery.

With my app, the seller uploads the voice notes and the app:

  1. Transcribes each note with Whisper.
  2. Extracts customer, item, quantity, unit, delivery date, address and notes with a Gemma model.
  3. Shows an editable order table, a CSV download, and a daily prep list that adds up how many of each item are due on each date.

The person who would pay for this is a home seller handling a steady stream of orders. They don't need a big business tool. They need something that saves an hour a day and doesn't send their customers' addresses to a stranger's server.

Demo

https://youtu.be/0M2gG12_r24

Code

laiba-Ashfaq / voice-order-taker

Voice Order Taker

https://voice-order-taker-jvh7zuvem9z6qbfuqfcvpm.streamlit.app/

Turn WhatsApp voice notes in Urdu, Roman Urdu, Pashto or English into a clean order sheet and a daily prep list. Everything runs on your own computer. No cloud, no API key, no per-order cost.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 2: Side Hustle).

The problem

Home bakers, tiffin services and small clothing sellers take most of their orders as WhatsApp voice notes. Someone says "do kilo chocolate cake aur teen dozen samosay kal shaam tak, house 12 Jinnah Road", and the seller has to replay it and write it down by hand. With 20 or more orders a week, this takes hours and mistakes happen.

What it does

  1. You upload one or more voice notes (.ogg, .opus, .m4a, .mp3, .wav).
  2. Whisper transcribes each note locally.
  3. A Gemma model running in Ollama extracts structured orders: customer, item, quantity…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Everything runs on a normal laptop with no cloud service.

  • faster-whisper (open-source Whisper) transcribes audio on the CPU. It reads WhatsApp .opus, .ogg and .m4a files directly.
  • Gemma, running locally through Ollama, reads the transcript and returns structured orders.
  • Streamlit is the interface, with a custom dark navy and teal theme and a CSS-only 3D robot mascot (no images or external libraries, so it works offline too).
  • pandas handles the editable table, the CSV export and the daily prep list.

The most important part was making a small model reliable. A free-form prompt gave me bad results, so I forced the output into a fixed JSON schema and added a worked example inside the prompt:

class OrderLine(BaseModel):
    customer: str = ""
    item: str = ""
    quantity: float = 1
    unit: str = ""
    delivery_date: str = ""
    address: str = ""
    notes: str = ""

class OrderList(BaseModel):
    orders: list[OrderLine]

r = ollama.chat(
    model=model,
    format=OrderList.model_json_schema(),
    options={"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 2048},
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system},
              {"role": "user", "content": transcript}],
)

The prompt also converts words like "kal" (tomorrow) and "parson" (day after tomorrow) into real dates, and I give Whisper a short list of dish names as an initial_prompt so it recognises local food words.

What went wrong along the way. I built this on a laptop with a nearly full C: drive and limited RAM, which turned out to be good testing for a "runs on cheap hardware" project:

  • The first model download failed because the disk was full, so I moved the model and cache folders to another drive.
  • A 6.6 GB Gemma model ran out of memory while Whisper was also loaded, so I switched to a smaller Gemma and reduced the context size.
  • A newer audio library version broke Whisper's decoder, so I pinned av<17.
  • My first extraction attempt with the smallest model returned a quantity with no item name. The schema and the worked example fixed most of that.

[Add your real numbers here, for example: "I tested X voice notes. N came out fully correct, M needed one edit, and K failed. Average time per note was about Y seconds on CPU."]

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this kind of customer, open models are not a nice extra. They are what makes the product possible.

  • Privacy. A voice note contains a customer's name, address and what they bought. With a closed API, all of that goes to a third-party server. Here it never leaves the seller's laptop.
  • Cost. Transcription and extraction cost nothing per order. A home baker can't justify per-minute and per-token fees, and a small flat monthly price still leaves a margin.
  • Offline use. Power and internet outages are common where I live. The app keeps working because nothing depends on a connection after the one-time model download.
  • Control. I could change the prompt, give Whisper local dish names, shrink the context, and swap one Gemma size for another when my laptop couldn't handle the bigger one. With a closed API, I would have been stuck with whatever the provider supports and charges.

The trade-off is honest too: a small local model is less accurate than a large cloud model on messy mixed-language speech, so the app always shows an editable table and the seller confirms the result before acting on it.
