articles.title: Don't Let the LLM Decide: How I Built a Predictable AI Tutor
articles.description: The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's...
articles.body_html:
The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's attempts and the answer. Tell it: "Help the learner, but don't give the answer away too early."

That works in a demo. It fails in an experiment. And it fails quietly in production too.

In the first post of this series I explained the experiment. I built an SQL tutor in two versions, called arms. Arm A makes you try before it helps, then gives a hint before the answer. Arm B gives the answer whenever you ask, like most AI tools. Six people used one or the other, then took a test a week later with no tutor.

This post is about how I built it. The core rule fits on one line:

The LLM never decides whether to help, or how much. Plain code decides. The LLM only writes the hint's wording, after that decision is made.

Why the LLM can't be the one deciding

Picture the prompt version. "If the learner seems stuck, give a hint. If they've really tried, give the answer."

Now try to answer one question: what did Arm A receive?

You can't. "Seems stuck" is a judgment the model makes fresh every time. Two learners in the same situation can get different help. The same learner can get different help on a retry. The thing you're trying to test becomes a moving target.

There's a second problem. With six people, there were only about 23 moments in the whole study where the tutor had to decide what help to give. You can't judge a model's decision-making from 23 examples. But you can fully test a plain function, and I did, with 123 unit tests.

So I split the system into three kinds of parts, a framing from my 100x Engineers AI course:

part does what why it sits there
human writes and runs SQL the skill being measured is theirs
deterministic (plain code) the try-first rule, the hint/answer rules, the answer checker, the leak guard the one thing being tested must be fixed and checkable
probabilistic (the LLM) writes the hint text, nothing else prose about this specific mistake is the one thing code can't write

The model is one small component. It's not the product.

The policy: a pure function

Here's the heart of policy.js, trimmed. No DOM, no network, no LLM. It takes the log for one question and returns an action.

const ACTION = {
  NONE:         'none',          // already solved
  REFUSE_GATE:  'refuse_gate',   // Arm A, no real attempt yet
  REFUSE_RETRY: 'refuse_retry',  // Arm A, hint given, keep trying
  HINT:         'hint',          // the LLM writes the text
  REVEAL:       'reveal',        // the reference query
};

const DEFAULT_N = 2; // attempts with the hint before the answer

function decide(item) {
  const N = item.N ?? DEFAULT_N;
  const counted = countableAttempts(item.attempts);
  const helpServed = item.helpServed || [];

  if (item.attempts.some(a => a.outcome === 'correct')) return { action: ACTION.NONE };

  // Arm B: the entire difference between the two groups is this line.
  if (item.arm === 'B') return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  // Arm A: the gate. No help of any kind until one attempt counts.
  if (counted.length === 0) return { action: ACTION.REFUSE_GATE };

  if (helpServed.some(h => h.action === ACTION.REVEAL)) return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  const hint = helpServed.find(h => h.action === ACTION.HINT);
  if (!hint) return { action: ACTION.HINT };

  const sinceHint = counted.length - hint.afterCountedAttempts;
  return sinceHint >= N ? { action: ACTION.REVEAL } : { action: ACTION.REFUSE_RETRY };
}

The only thing of interest here is the Arm B line. That one if is the whole difference between the two versions. Anyone can read it and know exactly what each group got.

Every decision is logged with counted and sinceHint. So for any Help press, I can look at the log and prove why the tutor responded the way it did.

N is fixed at 2 for everyone. If it changed per person, I'd be testing two things at once, and three people per group can't separate them.

What counts as an attempt?

Arm A's rule is "try first". I call it the gate: no help until you've made an attempt. So the code needs to decide what a real attempt is. This turned out to be the hardest part of the policy.

My first version said: an attempt counts if its result set is different from the last one. Simple, and wrong.

The bug: a query that doesn't run has no result set. So for a learner who couldn't get anything to execute, no attempt ever counted. The gate never opened. In my earlier test rounds, 101 of 122 attempts had a syntax error and didn't run. This wasn't an edge case. It was the main case.

And a query that fails to parse can still carry a full, wrong mental model:

SELECT customer, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 3

That doesn't run. It's also a perfect example of the exact mistake I was teaching about (filtering groups with WHERE instead of HAVING). It should count.

But asdf doesn't parse either. If junk counts, a learner can type three bits of junk and get a hint while thinking about nothing. Research on tutoring systems calls this "gaming the system", and learners find that shortcut fast.

So I added a substance bar. An attempt must contain one SQL keyword and one name from this question's schema:

function isSubstantive(sql, identifiers) {
  const low = String(sql ?? '').toLowerCase();
  if (!low.trim()) return false;
  if (!SQL_KEYWORDS.some(k => low.includes(k))) return false;
  if (!identifiers.length) return true; // fail open, see below
  return identifiers.some(id =>
    id.length >= 4
      ? low.includes(id)
      : new RegExp(`\\b${id}\\b`).test(low) // so "id" doesn't match "video"
  );
}

Matching is by substring on purpose. Real learners wrote GroupBy and havingcount>=3. That's mangled spelling, but a real mental model. A strict token match would throw those away.

I checked it against all 128 attempts from the screening round. 121 passed. The 7 rejected were 6 empty submissions and one bare SELECT. No real attempt was lost.

Notice the fail open line. If the schema list fails to load, the bar only checks for a keyword. A misconfigured page must not silently refuse every learner. That would turn Arm A into "no help at all" without anyone noticing.

The leak guard

Here's the uncomfortable part. To write a useful hint about a wrong query, the LLM has to see the correct one. I call that the reference query. So it's holding the answer while it writes. Sometimes it just prints it.

If that reaches the learner, Arm A quietly becomes Arm B on that question. The experiment stops testing anything, and nothing in the logs looks wrong.

So every hint passes through hint-guard.js before the learner sees it. It's deterministic. It makes no model calls. It looks at text and says yes or no.

function inspect(hint, { referenceQuery, learnerQuery }) {
  // 1. A runnable query: SELECT plus a real table after FROM/JOIN.
  // 2. A clause that distinguishes the reference query,
  //    unless the learner already wrote it themselves.
  // 3. Too much of the reference reproduced word for word.
  // 4. A walkthrough: four or more SQL keywords named.
}

If a hint is rejected, the system asks the model once more. If that fails too, it serves a hand-written fallback for that question. Every attempt and every rejection is logged.

Results: on 101 real hints, zero false alarms. Against 24 leaks I wrote specifically to beat it, it caught 22.

What can go wrong

Each rule in the guard exists because an earlier, simpler rule broke.

"SELECT and FROM means a leak." My first check rejected any hint containing both words. But they're normal English. "You started with SELECT, but where does the data come FROM?" is a great hint, and it got blocked. The fix: a runnable query must name a real table. The reference query tells you which tables exist, so look for those.

The semicolon rule. I also rejected "select ... ;" on the idea that a semicolon ends a statement. English uses semicolons too. "Nothing is processed; you need to say where the data comes from" got blocked. I deleted that rule instead of patching it, because the table rule already covered real queries.

Quoting the learner back to themselves. The prompt asks the model to quote what the learner wrote. So a hint would say "your MAX(price) is fine". MAX(price) is part of the answer, so the guard blocked it. 7 of 8 rejections in one test run were this. But the learner already wrote it. It's in their editor. Now a clause only counts as a leak if the learner doesn't already have it.

The leak with no SQL in it. "The FROM keyword picks the products table, then GROUP BY groups the rows by category..." No clause appears verbatim, but you could type the answer straight from it. The signal is shape, not content. A real hint talks about one or two things. A dictation names everything.

I didn't pick the threshold by feel. I measured it. Across the 101 real hints: 66 named no SQL keyword, 29 named one, 5 named two, 1 named three, and none named four. The two prose leaks named six and seven. A limit of four separates them with room on both sides.

The silent fallback. The LLM sits behind a Supabase edge function, so the API key never reaches the browser. Supabase pauses free projects after about a week without traffic. When paused, nothing errors. Arm A just serves the hand-written backup hints. The app looks fine, but it's quietly running a different tutor. I found this once, fixed it, and added a script to check it before every session.

What this means for your code

If you're putting an LLM into a product, ask one question about each decision: does this need judgment, or does it need to be the same every time?

  • If the behaviour has to be explainable, testable or consistent, it belongs in code.
  • If it needs language about this specific case, that's what the model is for.
  • Put a deterministic check between the model and the user for anything that would be expensive if the model got it wrong.

In my tutor, that split is why I could say exactly what each group got. It's also why the experiment could fail honestly. When two of my checks failed, I knew the failure was about learners, not about a model behaving differently on a Tuesday.

Next in the series: the mistakes I made running my first controlled experiment as a developer, including the one a Demo Day judge caught.

vikrantnegi / withholding-pilot

Learning OS — 100x Cohort 7 final capstone

Vikrant Negi. Solo. Demo Day track. Submission 7 Oct 2026.

An SQL tutor that makes you try before it helps, and a 6-person pilot testing whether that changes what you can do a week later, with the tutor gone.

For where things stand today, read STATUS.md. That is the only file that claims to be current.

Try it

Live app: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/

  • Withholding tutor: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/index.html?arm=A
  • Answer-giving baseline: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/index.html?arm=B

What each one does:

  • ?arm=A opens the withholding tutor. Press Help before trying, and it refuses. Try once, and Help gives a hint. Two more tries, and it gives the answer.
  • ?arm=B opens the baseline. Help gives the full answer at once.

Same page, same 16 practice questions, same grader. One config flag is the only difference.

The result

Arm A scored 36 of 36 person-questions (3 learners x 12 held-out questions). Arm…

View on GitHub

Try both arms live: Arm A · Arm B

articles.title: How a power station runtime estimate is computed (and why it rounds down)
articles.description: A portable power station says "1,000 Wh" on the box, but nobody gets 1,000 Wh of AC output from it....
articles.body_html:
A portable power station says "1,000 Wh" on the box, but nobody gets 1,000 Wh of AC output from it. While building a runtime calculator, I had to decide how to turn a spec sheet into a number people can plan around. Here is the model I ended up with, and why every choice leans conservative.

The core idea: subtract losses, then divide

Runtime is just energy divided by power. The work is in being honest about both sides of that division.

Energy side. The rated watt-hours are measured at the cell level. You can't pull all of it out: the battery management system stops discharge before the cells are truly empty. I default to using 90% of rated capacity.

Power side. If your load is an AC device, the inverter has to convert DC from the battery. Inverters aren't perfect, so I assume 88% efficiency. The inverter also burns power just by being switched on, even with nothing plugged in. I assume a 10 W idle draw and add it to the load.

The formula 

function runtimeHours({ ratedWh, loadW, usableShare = 0.9, inverterEff = 0.88, idleW = 10 }) {
  const usableWh = ratedWh * usableShare;
  const drawW = loadW / inverterEff + idleW;   // what the battery really supplies
  return Math.floor((usableWh / drawW) * 10) / 10; // always round down
}

runtimeHours({ ratedWh: 1000, loadW: 100 }); // 7.2 h, not 10 h

For a 100 W load on a 1,000 Wh unit: usable energy is 900 Wh, the battery supplies about 123.6 W (100 / 0.88 + 10), so you get 7.28 hours, which floors to 7.2. It is nowhere near the 10 hours the naive division suggests.

Fridges are not constant loads

A fridge's nameplate wattage is what it draws while the compressor runs. The compressor cycles, so over a day it runs about a third of the time. I model that as a duty cycle of roughly 33%:

const fridgeAvgW = fridgeRunningW * 0.33;

Treating a 150 W fridge as a constant 150 W would underestimate runtime by a factor of three. Treating it as 50 W forever ignores startup surge, which is a separate check on whether the inverter can start the compressor at all.

One number is a lie, so show a range

Real conditions vary: temperature, battery age, how hard devices actually pull. Instead of a single figure I output three:

  • Cautious: pushes the assumptions the wrong way (lower usable share, lower efficiency, higher idle draw).
  • Typical: the defaults above.
  • Optimistic: assumptions nudged the other way. 
const scenarios = {
  cautious:   { usableShare: 0.85, inverterEff: 0.85, idleW: 15 },
  typical:    { usableShare: 0.90, inverterEff: 0.88, idleW: 10 },
  optimistic: { usableShare: 0.95, inverterEff: 0.92, idleW: 8 },
};

The spread is the useful part. If the cautious case still covers your outage, you're fine. If only the optimistic one does, you know to buy more capacity or cut loads.

Why always round down

Rounding a runtime up by even half an hour can mean a CPAP machine or a router dies at 3 a.m. Rounding down costs the user nothing but a little pessimism. I apply Math.floor at the very last step, never in the middle of the calculation, so errors don't compound.

Things I deliberately don't do

  • I don't invent numbers. If a manufacturer doesn't publish a spec, the field stays empty rather than being guessed.
  • I don't hide defaults. Every assumption is printed next to the result so you can disagree with it.

Try it

I put this model into a free calculator, Kilohour, so you can check the math against your own devices. If you think any default is off, I'd like to hear which one and why. These are defaults, not laws of physics, and measured data from real units would improve them.

articles.title: Your WebRTC viewer says connected. The picture is frozen.
articles.description: There is a failure mode in WebRTC that looks healthy from almost every...
articles.body_html:
There is a failure mode in WebRTC that looks healthy from almost every angle:

pc.iceConnectionState === "connected";
pc.connectionState === "connected";
video.readyState === HTMLMediaElement.HAVE_ENOUGH_DATA;

The signaling socket is open. The peer connection has a candidate pair. The video
element is attached. And the frame on screen has not moved for three minutes.

That last sentence is the problem. connected describes the transport, not the
picture. A media track can be live while no new frames are rendered.

Try the freeze-and-recovery demo in your browser. It freezes a real media stream, shows Transport: connected throughout the outage, then walks through ICE restart and full rejoin. No install and no account.

Frames are the health check

If the audience is watching video, the useful health signal is not a connection state.
It is an advancing frame.

requestVideoFrameCallback gives us that signal. It fires when the browser has a new
video frame to present, and its metadata includes the presentation time:

video.requestVideoFrameCallback((now, metadata) => {
  console.log(metadata.presentationTime, metadata.width, metadata.height);
});

That one callback can drive both recovery and observability: the viewer is healthy when
frames are arriving, and it is frozen when they stop.

Older browsers may not implement the callback. There, a timer can watch
video.currentTime. It is less precise, but it still distinguishes playback from a
still image.

Recover in the cheapest order

When frames stop, the instinct is to tear down and reconnect everything. That works,
but it is the most expensive option: a new socket, a new offer, a new answer and a new
peer connection. Most interruptions do not require all of that.

I use a three-step recovery ladder:

  1. ICE restart. Reuse the current session and negotiate new candidates. This is usually enough after a Wi-Fi change or a network path failure.
  2. Full rejoin. Replace the signaling session and peer connection. This covers server-side sessions that went stale or a publisher that republished.
  3. Backoff and retry. Repeating full rejoins without a delay can turn one broken client into a retry storm.

The deadlines matter. A restart that has not produced a new frame in five seconds is
not a successful restart. A rejoin that has not produced a new frame in eight seconds
is not a successful rejoin. The transition should be driven by rendered frames, not by
the fact that a connection event fired.

A compact implementation

I published the recovery logic as webrtc-recovery. It contains no signaling or media
server code; you provide restart() and rejoin() for your own stack.

import { createRecoveryLadder, watchFrames } from "webrtc-recovery";

const ladder = createRecoveryLadder({
  restart: () => signaling.send({ type: "restart" }),
  rejoin: () => {
    pc.close();
    pc = null;
    signaling.reconnect();
  },
});

watchFrames(video, {
  onStall: () => ladder.onIceState("failed"),
  onResume: () => ladder.markHealthy(),
});

video.requestVideoFrameCallback(function tick() {
  ladder.markHealthy("frame");
  video.requestVideoFrameCallback(tick);
});

The important part is the invariant: only a rendered frame clears the recovery
deadline. A successful setRemoteDescription or an iceConnectionState transition is
not evidence that somebody can see the stream.

The package is ESM-only, has zero runtime dependencies, and the state machine accepts
an injected clock, so the timeout branches can be tested without real waits. The
current release is available from GitHub while the npm listing is being prepared:

npm install https://github.com/AiLaoHuYu/webrtc-recovery/archive/refs/tags/v0.1.1.tar.gz

Repository:
https://github.com/AiLaoHuYu/webrtc-recovery

Diagnose one thing, not ten numbers

getStats() can return dozens of numbers at once. A viewer does not need a dashboard;
it needs the first useful explanation.

Check the highest-severity condition first:

  1. Is the transport failed or closed?
  2. Is the frame watchdog reporting a stall?
  3. Is packet loss already bad enough to explain poor quality?
  4. Is the jitter buffer growing?
  5. Is the sender capped by bandwidth or CPU?
  6. Is signaling up but no frame dimensions arriving?

That ordering avoids the common mistake of telling a user about 3% packet loss while
the real problem is that the peer connection is dead.

The same package exposes sampleConnection() to flatten a stats report and
diagnose() to turn the first actionable condition into one sentence.

What this does not solve

Client recovery cannot fix a server that is down, a publisher that stopped sending
media, or a TURN service with no capacity. It also cannot make an expired signaling
session valid.

What it can do is stop a viewer from sitting on a frozen frame while every status badge
says everything is fine. In a live video product, that difference is the whole user
experience.

If you are assembling the rest of the stack yourself, the library and source are here:

https://github.com/AiLaoHuYu/webrtc-recovery

If you would rather start from the full self-hosted WebRTC video server, including
signaling, the SFU, the publisher and the viewer, see https://lowlatencykit.com.
The complete source package is also available through
Codester.

articles.title: Rename the Variable, Change the Security Verdict
articles.description: One of my own rules flags a Zod schema containing no XPath, and stays silent on textbook XPath injection. Both come from the same heuristic: it decides whether a value is attacker-controlled by substring-matching the variable's name.
articles.body_html:
Four lines, run through my own XPath injection rule today:

xpath.select("//user[@id='" + id     + "']", doc);   // silent
xpath.select("//user[@id='" + userId + "']", doc);   // FIRES

export const QueryValidateSchema = QueryInputSchema; // FIRES
export const SchemaA             = SchemaB;          // silent

The first two are the same vulnerability. The last two are the same statement.
The only thing that changed is what the variables are called.

The heuristic

no-xpath-injection has to decide whether a value is attacker-controlled. Here
is how it decides:

const varName = inputNode.name.toLowerCase();
if (["req", "request", "query", "params", "input", "user", "search"]
      .some((keyword) => varName.includes(keyword))) {
  return true;   // tainted
}

That is the whole test. Not where the value came from — what it is spelled.

Both errors, one cause

The false positive. QueryInputSchema lowercases to queryinputschema,
which contains query and also input. Tainted. There is no XPath call in
that statement at all — it is a Zod schema being re-exported. The rule reports
an injection risk on an assignment.

The false negative. id contains none of the seven substrings, so the
value is not tainted, so a concatenation flowing into xpath.select — a sink
this rule already recognises, it is in the default xpathFunctions list — is
not reported. Textbook XPath injection, silently accepted.

The //user[...] string does contain user. It does not matter: the check
runs on the identifier, never on the literal.

One predicate, opposite failures. That is what makes this a single defect
rather than two bugs that happen to share a file.

Why this is worse than being wrong

A rule with a 70% false-positive rate is annoying and legible — you read the
findings, you see the noise, you tune it or drop it.

This is not that. This rule is right about the shape of the problem and
wrong about the input to it, which means its errors correlate with naming
conventions rather than with code. A codebase that says userInput gets
flagged everywhere. A codebase that says val, x, raw or id gets a clean
report and the same vulnerabilities.

Two teams, identical risk, opposite verdicts — and neither has any way to tell
from the output which one they are.

It also fails toward silence in exactly the case that matters. Short, neutral
identifiers are what you find in the compact, clever code most likely to be
doing something sharp with strings.

What it should read instead

The value's origin, not its spelling. Did it come from a request handler
parameter, a process.argv, a req.* member, a function boundary the rule
cannot see past? That is
taint analysis,
and it is more expensive than a substring match — which is precisely why the
substring match was written.

The honest framing is that this rule is a heuristic wearing a taint rule's
messaging. The fix is not a longer keyword list. A longer list moves the
boundary; it does not stop the verdict being a function of names.

The check that finds these

Take any rule you rely on. Write the vulnerable case. Then rename every
identifier in it to a single letter and run it again.

If the verdict changes, the rule is reading names. You now know something about
your tooling that no amount of reading its findings would have told you —
because a finding you never get is indistinguishable from a clean file, and
precision and recall measured on a corpus that shares your naming conventions will both look fine.
It is the same reason a labelled fixture set catches what unit tests miss:
the tests assert the rule's behaviour on the names its author chose.

This is a known class in our own tracker, with a lint check that gates new
occurrences and a documented list of the ones still outstanding. This rule is
on that list. Measured against the workspace build of
eslint-plugin-secure-coding
today — if you are on the published release, re-run before assuming.

The rule is
no-xpath-injection;
the predicate is in
its source.
Both are open, which is the only reason this article can be specific.

⭐ Star the repo if you would rather find your linter's blind spots in an article than in an incident.

eslint-plugin-secure-coding is part of the Interlace ESLint ecosystem. Source on GitHub · Follow: Dev.to/ofri-peretz

Rename the variables in your worst file to single letters. Does your linter still find the bug?

articles.title: A financial calculator is only as good as its formula
articles.description: Online financial calculators have a trust problem. You type in your numbers, a monthly payment...
articles.body_html:
Online financial calculators have a trust problem. You type in your numbers, a monthly payment appears, and you have no idea what math produced it. Was that mortgage calc using monthly or semi-annual compounding? Does the tax calculator include state tax? Which year's brackets? Usually, you can't tell — the formula is hidden.

I think the fix is embarrassingly simple: publish the formula. Here's what that looks like in practice, from building a set of financial calculators.

Show the math on the page

Every calculator should display the actual formula it uses, with the variables labeled. For compound interest, that's A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) — and then define each symbol in plain language. This does two things: users can verify the result by hand, and other developers can spot your mistakes. Both have happened to me, and both made the tool better.

State your assumptions explicitly

A mortgage calculator isn't just a formula — it's a stack of assumptions: compounding frequency, whether property tax and insurance are included, how extra payments are applied. List them next to the result. The calculators people trust most are the ones that say "here's what I assumed" instead of pretending there's one true answer.

Run it client-side

Financial numbers are sensitive. Running the calculation entirely in the browser means the numbers never leave the user's device — there's no server log of someone's salary or mortgage balance to leak. As a bonus, results update instantly as you type, which makes the tool feel dramatically better.

Test against known values

Before shipping, verify each calculator against authoritative sources: IRS tax tables for the income tax calc, bank-published amortization examples for mortgages. Write these as actual test cases, not eyeball checks. One wrong assumption in a refinance calculator can cost a real person real money.

Write guides, not just inputs

Most people don't know what "points" or "PMI" mean. A short plain-English explanation next to each input turns a calculator from a black box into a learning tool — and it's what separates a useful page from a commodity widget.

I applied all of this building CalcWise (https://finance.toppn.com/) — 9 free financial calculators covering compound interest, mortgage, refinance, credit-card payoff, retirement, investing, income tax, ROI and profit margin. Formulas published, everything runs locally in the browser, no sign-up. The most valuable feedback I've gotten wasn't feature requests — it was people checking my math. That's exactly the dynamic you want.

articles.title: PHP 8.6 Adds foo(?, 2) Partial Application. Here's How to Write It in TypeScript
articles.description: PHP 8.6's ? and ... placeholders mapped to TypeScript: arrow closures, bind() and its limits, and a typed partial() built on variadic tuples.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The PHP 8.5 release page shows off the new pipe operator with this chain:

$slug = $title
    |> trim(...)
    |> (fn($str) => str_replace(' ', '-', $str))
    |> (fn($str) => str_replace('.', '', $str))
    |> strtolower(...);

Two of those four steps are arrow functions whose only job is to move $str into the third slot of str_replace(). In PHP 8.6 each one shrinks to str_replace(' ', '-', ?). The Partial Function Application v2 RFC by Larry Garfield and Arnaud Le Blanc closed its vote on December 5, 2025, adopted 33-0-0, targeting PHP 8.6. That release is already in release candidates, so its feature set is frozen: the php.net archive shows RC3 out on October 8.

If you write PHP by day and TypeScript the rest of the time, the next question is what the same move looks like on the other side. There are three answers, and each one gives up something PHP's version keeps.

What ? and ... do in PHP 8.6

A call with at least one placeholder doesn't run the function. It returns a Closure. ? stands for exactly one argument. ... stands for zero or more and can appear once, at the end. Positional values and ? come first, named arguments after. The closure copies the real function's parameter types, names and return type.

function fee(int $cents, float $rate, string $currency): string
{
    return sprintf('%.2f %s', $cents * $rate / 100, $currency);
}

$eur    = fee(?, 0.029, 'EUR');         // fn(int $cents)
$at1999 = fee(1999, ?, 'EUR');          // fn(float $rate)
$tail   = fee(1999, ...);               // fn(float, string)
$thunk  = fee(1999, 0.029, 'EUR', ...); // fn(): string

// Named placeholders: the closure takes (currency, cents)
$byName = fee(currency: ?, cents: ?, rate: 0.029);

echo $eur(1999); // 0.58 EUR

Two details matter for the TypeScript side. First, bound arguments are evaluated when the partial is created, not when it's called. The RFC contrasts the two forms with an example of this shape:

// currentRate() runs once, right here
$partial = fee(?, currentRate(), 'EUR');

// currentRate() runs on every call
$arrow = fn(int $c) => fee($c, currentRate(), 'EUR');

Second, a follow-up RFC on optional parameters, accepted 25-0 with one abstention in May 2026, makes every parameter created by ? required, even when the original had a default. Parameters pulled in by ... keep their optionality.

The arrow function is the TypeScript default

TypeScript has no placeholder syntax, so the everyday answer is the thing PHP 8.6 replaces: a closure that forwards.

function fee(cents: number, rate: number, currency: string) {
  return `${((cents * rate) / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;
}

const eurFee = (cents: number) => fee(cents, 0.029, "EUR");
const rateFor1999 = (rate: number) => fee(1999, rate, "EUR");
const thunkFee = () => fee(1999, 0.029, "EUR");

console.log(eurFee(1999)); // 0.58 EUR

It covers every PHP form: a hole at the front, a hole in the middle, a zero-argument thunk. What it costs is repetition. You restate each open parameter's type by hand, and if fee changes its signature, the wrapper's annotation is one more place to update.

It also evaluates lazily, like PHP's arrow form and unlike fee(?, ...). There's one more difference a PHP developer will trip on: PHP arrow functions capture outer variables by value when they're created, while a JavaScript closure reads the variable itself, so it sees every later reassignment.

bind() only fills the front

The built-in alternative is Function.prototype.bind. Since TypeScript 3.2, the strictBindCallApply option (part of strict) types it properly instead of returning any.

const forCents = fee.bind(null, 1999);
// takes (rate, currency), returns string

console.log(forCents(0.029, "EUR")); // 0.58 EUR

The typing comes from CallableFunction in the lib.es5.d.ts declarations, where bind is declared over a function with parameters [...A, ...B]: A is what you pass, B is what's left. That gets you PHP's fee(1999, ...) with correct types.

It stops there. bind only fills arguments from the left, so fee(?, 0.029, 'EUR') has no bind equivalent. You always pass a this value, even for a plain function. And the 3.2 release notes named two limits at launch: generic functions lost their type parameters, and for an overloaded function only the last overload is modeled.

A typed partial() with a placeholder

You can get the middle-of-the-list hole back with a placeholder value and some type-level work. Lodash's _.partial accepts _ as a placeholder; what follows is a small typed version built on the variadic tuple types TypeScript 4.0 introduced and the conditional-type infer keyword that has been around since TypeScript 2.8.

Save this as partial.ts:

export {};

const _ = Symbol("placeholder");
type _ = typeof _;

type Arr = readonly unknown[];

// Each argument is either a real value or the placeholder.
type Slots<P extends Arr> = { [K in keyof P]: P[K] | _ };

// Walk params and args together; keep params that got a _.
type Holes<P extends Arr, A extends Arr> =
  A extends readonly [infer AH, ...infer AT]
    ? P extends readonly [infer PH, ...infer PT]
      ? AH extends _
        ? [PH, ...Holes<PT, AT>]
        : Holes<PT, AT>
      : []
    : P;

function partial<P extends Arr, R, A extends Slots<P>>(
  f: (...args: P) => R,
  ...args: A
): (...rest: Holes<P, A>) => R;
function partial(f: (...a: any[]) => any, ...args: any[]) {
  return (...rest: any[]) => {
    let i = 0;
    const full = args.map((a) => (a === _ ? rest[i++] : a));
    return f(...full, ...rest.slice(i));
  };
}

function fee(cents: number, rate: number, currency: string) {
  return `${((cents * rate) / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;
}

const eur = partial(fee, _, 0.029, "EUR");   // (cents) => string
const at1999 = partial(fee, 1999, _, "EUR"); // (rate) => string
const twoHoles = partial(fee, _, 0.029, _);  // (cents, currency)

console.log(eur(1999));              // 0.58 EUR
console.log(at1999(0.035));          // 0.70 EUR
console.log(twoHoles(10000, "USD")); // 2.90 USD

// partial(fee, _, "0.029", "EUR"); // type error: not a number
// partial(fee, _, 0.029);          // type error: 3 slots needed

Slots<P> is a mapped type over the parameter tuple, so every position accepts its real type or _. Because A must fit all of Slots<P>, leaving a slot out is a compile error, which matches PHP throwing ArgumentCountError for a ?-only call that doesn't cover the required parameters. Holes<P, A> walks both tuples one element at a time with infer and keeps the parameter types that sat under a _. That tuple becomes the rest parameter of the returned function.

The implementation signature uses any on purpose. The public overload carries the types; the body only swaps placeholders for incoming arguments in order and appends anything extra.

PHP's fee(1999, ...) form doesn't need a placeholder at all. The partialCall example from the TypeScript 4.0 notes already covers it, and with every argument supplied it gives you a thunk:

function partialHead<H extends Arr, T extends Arr, R>(
  f: (...args: [...H, ...T]) => R,
  ...head: H
): (...tail: T) => R {
  return (...tail: T) => f(...head, ...tail);
}

const later = partialHead(fee, 1999, 0.029, "EUR"); // () => string
console.log(later()); // 0.58 EUR

Both helpers evaluate bound arguments at creation time, like PHP. Append this to the file to see the difference from a closure:

let rate = 0.029;
const bound = partial(fee, _, rate, "EUR");
const live = (cents: number) => fee(cents, rate, "EUR");
rate = 0.05;

console.log(bound(10000)); // 2.90 EUR: rate read at creation
console.log(live(10000));  // 5.00 EUR: rate read at call time

Run it with tsx:

npx tsx partial.ts
npx -p typescript tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 partial.ts

The second command matters. tsx strips types and runs the file, and its docs say plainly that it does not type-check your code. The two commented-out bad calls only fail under tsc.

Where PHP's version still wins

Named arguments. fee(currency: ?, cents: ?, rate: 0.029) works on the original function. TypeScript has no named arguments, so the closest you get is an options object and a helper that fixes some keys:

type FeeArgs = { cents: number; rate: number; currency: string };

const feeOf = ({ cents, rate, currency }: FeeArgs) =>
  fee(cents, rate, currency);

function fix<O extends object, K extends keyof O, R>(
  f: (opts: O) => R,
  fixed: Pick<O, K>,
): (rest: Omit<O, K>) => R {
  return (rest) => f({ ...fixed, ...rest } as O);
}

const usd = fix(feeOf, { currency: "USD" });
console.log(usd({ cents: 10000, rate: 0.029 })); // 2.90 USD

It works, but you had to change the function's shape to get there, and the as O cast is there because the compiler can't prove that Pick<O, K> plus Omit<O, K> adds back up to O.

Signature fidelity. PHP's closure copies names, types and by-reference parameters from the real function (defaults too, for parameters pulled in by ...), and named placeholders can reorder them. The Holes tuple keeps types but not parameter names, so editor hints get vaguer than the original.

Overloads and this. When TypeScript infers from an overloaded function, the handbook says inferences come from the last signature, and that applies to partial() as much as to bind. The helper also drops this, while the RFC lets you partially apply methods, static methods and invokable objects directly.

Syntax. In PHP, ? is part of the language, and the RFC says the compiler turns some pipe forms such as foo(?) into direct calls. In TypeScript, every partial() is a runtime closure plus an array walk.

TypeScript's advantage is the compile-time check: the two commented-out calls at the bottom of partial.ts show up red in your editor before anything runs.

For most code, the arrow function is still the right TypeScript answer. It's one line, and there's nothing to explain in review. Reach for partial() when you're building callbacks in a loop or feeding a pipeline and the hole sits in the middle of the argument list.

If this was useful

This post is one feature mapped across two languages, with the places where the mapping leaks. That's what PHP to TypeScript does for a whole PHP 8+ habit set: sync-to-async, generics and discriminated unions. It's part of The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you came here from PHP, PHP to TypeScript stands in for the first book, and The TypeScript Type System is where Slots and Holes stop looking like magic. Shipping TypeScript at work already? Add TypeScript in Production. The whole set is at xgabriel.com/the-typescript-library.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Sending transactional email from Node.js in Ghana (and paying with mobile money)
articles.description: Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The...
articles.body_html:
Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The usual answer is SendGrid, Mailgun or Resend, and they're good services. But if you're building in Ghana, you hit the same wall I did: they're priced in dollars and want an international card.

So I built Sankofa, an email API that's prepaid in cedis. You top up with MTN MoMo, Telecel Cash or AirtelTigo Money at GHS 5 per 1,000 emails, with no subscription.

This post walks through sending email from a Node.js app with it, from your first test email to bulk sends and delivery webhooks.

1. Get an API key

Create an account, then open API Keys in the dashboard and create one. It starts with esk_ and is shown once, so put it straight into your environment:

export SANKOFA_API_KEY=esk_your_api_key

Keep it on your server. Never put it in frontend code, where anyone can read it.

2. Send your first email (no DNS needed)

Normally you can't send email until you've verified a domain. To get you going sooner, every account can use a shared test sender, hello@test.trysankofa.com, which can only send to the email address you signed up with:

const response = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "hello@test.trysankofa.com",
    to: "you@example.com", // the address you signed up with
    subject: "Hello from my app",
    text: "It works!",
  }),
});

const body = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${body.error}: ${body.message}`);
console.log("Sent:", body.messageId);

That uses the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later, so there's nothing to install. Check your inbox, and your spam folder the first time.

3. Send from your own domain

When you're ready to email your users, verify your domain on the Domains page. Sankofa gives you three DNS records to add. Once they're in, you can send from any address on that domain:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your order has shipped",
    html: "<p>Your order is on its way.</p>",
    text: "Your order is on its way.",
  }),
});

Each recipient uses one credit. If a send fails, the credit comes back automatically.

4. Templates, and sending to many people

For emails you send repeatedly, save a template with {{placeholders}}:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/templates", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    name: "order-shipped",
    subject: "Your order {{order}} has shipped",
    text: "Hi {{name}}, your order {{order}} is on its way.",
  }),
});

Then send it to up to 500 people in one request. Each person gets their own copy with their own values filled in:

const result = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails/bulk", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    templateName: "order-shipped",
    recipients: [
      { to: "ama@example.com", templateData: { name: "Ama", order: "A-1042" } },
      { to: "kofi@example.com", templateData: { name: "Kofi", order: "A-1043" } },
    ],
  }),
}).then((r) => r.json());

for (const r of result.results) console.log(r.to, r.status, r.error ?? "");

If one recipient fails (say, an address that bounced before), the rest still go out, and you're not charged for the failure.

5. Know when emails are delivered

Register a webhook on the Webhooks page, and Sankofa will POST delivery events to your server: delivered, bounced, opened, clicked and so on. Each request is signed, so check the signature before trusting it:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export function isFromSankofa(rawBody, signatureHeader, secret) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(signatureHeader.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")));
  if (!parts.t || !parts.v1) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) > 300) return false; // reject old requests

  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${parts.t}.${rawBody}`).digest();
  const given = Buffer.from(parts.v1, "hex");
  return given.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, expected);
}

Pass it the raw request body (before JSON parsing) and the X-Webhook-Signature header.

Bonus: let your AI assistant send email

Sankofa has an MCP server, so tools like Claude Code and Cursor can send email and check delivery for you. Create a separate API key for the agent and give it a daily limit, so it can never send more than you allow:

claude mcp add --transport http sankofa https://api.trysankofa.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer esk_your_agent_key"

Then you can ask, "email the team that the deploy is done", and it will.

Wrapping up

That covers most of what an app needs: test sends, your own domain, templates, bulk sends and delivery tracking. The docs cover the rest, including attachments and receiving replies.

It's early days, so I'd really value feedback, especially from anyone building in Ghana or elsewhere in West Africa. What do you use for email today, and what would make you switch?

The first 20 developers get 200 free emails to try it.
